Everyone is asking who will win the AI race. During yesterday’s IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit in New York, I posed a different question: what does winning actually mean?

For me, the answer starts with energy.

AI could help unlock up to 175 GW of capacity from existing transmission lines. Across the Global South, companies are already using it for grid optimisation, smart metering, forecasting and industrial efficiency.

But the same technology can push in the opposite direction. AI is also making oil and gas exploration faster and cheaper, with recent modelling suggesting the resulting emissions could be 3.3 to 13.3 times larger than estimated 2025 data-centre emissions.

So the question is not whether AI is efficient. It is what AI is making more efficient.

This matters when 91% of new utility-scale renewable projects are already cheaper than the cheapest new fossil alternative. In Pakistan, low-cost solar imports helped avoid more than $12 billion in fuel imports. In Chile, financing for the 151 MW Calama wind farm was linked to emissions avoided through early coal retirement.

AI will add another major source of electricity demand. Whether that extends the age of energy addition or accelerates the transition will depend on choices around grids, finance, standards and public policy.

And who captures the value?

Middle-income countries generate more than 40% of ChatGPT traffic, yet middle- and low-income countries host only around 27% of shared data-centre facilities.

A sustainable AI framework must therefore ask what AI enables across the economy, where infrastructure is built, who owns the capabilities, and what countries gain in return.

Human intelligence created this wave. The task now is to decide where we direct it.

We explore these questions further in UNDP’s The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries? https://lnkd.in/gUFFVVgS #EnergyforDevelopment #NewYorkClimateWeek

74% of participants wanted to explore clean energy careers. 56% asked how to start.

These are findings from UNDP and Goodwall’s conversations with more than 58,000 young people across over 180 countries. One participant described people travelling long distances just to charge their devices. With 655 million people still without electricity, that journey says a great deal about who can access the digital economy.

Today, we brought public and private sector partners together to discuss how to close the skills gap and bring clean energy jobs to places that need them most.

Renewable energy already employs 16.6 million people, but more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in five countries and regions. The talent is far more widely distributed.

Young people proposed businesses ranging from solar-powered kitchens to sustainable energy consultancies. They also asked for practical ways to learn the skills those ideas require. UNDP’s upcoming Sustainable Energy Academy will offer more than 40 hours of modules spanning energy finance and governance, access and efficiency, data and technology, and the climate-energy nexus.

As a young man from the Philippines told us: “Invest not only in clean energy technologies, but also in the young people who build them. Because when we power communities with clean energy, we don't just light homes, we ignite opportunities.”

Every year of delay leaves communities without reliable power and holds back the people ready to build a cleaner energy future.

Tomorrow, UNDP and Goodwall will release "Powering the Future," our full report on the careers young people want to pursue, the businesses they want to build, and what they need to get started. #CleanEnergyJobs #YouthEmployment #EnergyAccess #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

A.C.C.T© Forum: Advancing Africa’s Clean Cooking Transition Through Solutions, Finance & Collaboration

The African Clean Cooking Transition Forum (ACCT©) brought together policymakers, government leaders, development partners, energy experts, innovators and civil society leaders to address one of Africa’s most pressing energy-access challenges: accelerating the transition to clean cooking.

The forum opened with remarks from Mr. Louis Cheick SISSOKO, Presiding Officer of the African Union ECOSOCC), followed by reflections from the Forum Chair, H.E Ambassador Prof. Olufolake Abdulrazaq, and Co-Chair, H.E. Ms. Macenje Mazoka .

A central panel discussion, “Solutions and Financing for Clean Cooking in Africa,” examined the role of innovation, investment, financing mechanisms and practical delivery models in expanding access to clean cooking. 

The discussion was moderated by Joy Osomiamhe-O, Executive Director of G-SEL Network and Convener of the ACCT© Forum.

The programme also featured a keynote address by Mr. Riad Meddeb of UNDP, alongside ministerial and goodwill remarks from government leaders across Nigeria, Mozambique and Tanzania.

A key highlight was the presentation of the Lagos State Clean Cooking Pilot by Mrs. Titilayo Oshodi MCIPM, FISMN, demonstrating how subnational action and innovative approaches can contribute to the wider clean cooking transition.

The forum concluded with a signing ceremony and commitments toward continued collaboration, followed by closing remarks and next steps from the Convener.

The ACCT© Forum reinforced an important message: the transition to clean cooking requires more than commitments—it requires finance, innovation, policy, partnerships and solutions that can reach the households and communities that need them.

G-SEL Network remains committed to convening the conversations and partnerships needed to turn these commitments into meaningful impact.

🏝️ One of Sicily's main cities just did something no municipality has done before.
 
🤝 Agrigento has signed on to become the first local administration in the world to join the 100x100 Campaign, applying the same island-led approach that's driving renewable transitions from Curaçao to Tonga, to a mainland Italian town.
 
⚡ The city faces real pressure: recurring power outages, wildfires straining the grid, energy prices above the EU average, all set against the backdrop of the Valley of the Temples.
 
🎯 Rather than wait, Agrigento is taking the lead, committing to 100% renewable energy by 2045 or sooner, guided by Greening the Islands Foundation and Blue Planet Alliance through a comprehensive roadmap covering technology, policy and finance, and its hands-on implementation on the ground, setting an example for Sicily and for towns across Italy and beyond.
 
🌍 This is what bottom up climate governance looks like: local communities, who understand their own vulnerabilities best, driving the solutions.
 
✍️ The MoU was signed in New York during Climate Week, making Agrigento the first municipality to join as a case study of a local community taking the lead on its own energy transition towards 100% RES, an approach welcomed by International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), UNDP, Global Solar Council (GSC) and Global Renewables Alliance (GRA).

Yesterday, at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) we published the third edition of the Tracking report on the UAE Consensus goals, and I've been going back through it.

The headline is good news, with a record of 693 GW of renewable capacity added in 2025, and the gap to tripling by 2030 narrowed to about 0.6 TW.

The part I keep coming back to is further in, and is bringing some hope to all of us working on accelerating a renewables-powered energy transition: 
- Factories can now make more than twice as many solar modules as the world is buying.
- Most new renewable capacity is cheaper than the cheapest fossil alternative. 

The technology is there, and it's cheap.

And yet, of those 693 GW, Africa added 11.3. Central and West Africa together added 0.4, while G20 countries account for around 91% of the investment.

So in a lot of these markets the problem isn't the price of panels. It's the price of money. 

The report is direct about it: country, currency and regulatory risk keep capital away, and what helps is guarantees, de-risking, concessional finance and buyers for the power that a lender can trust.

For those of you on the financing side: in your experience, what moves things more in these markets: is it a cheaper capital, or a more reliable buyer for the power?

Source: IRENA (2026), Delivering on the UAE Consensus

HOT OFF THE PRESS: For the first time ever, the IEA has published a dedicated Electrification Report. It is an absolute treasure trove of data. Here are some of the key takeaways that stood out to me when I peer-reviewed it.

1) Electrofficiency: The headline electrification rate undersells electricity's real role. Electricity is 23% of final energy, but it delivers almost 40% of useful energy - the heat, mobility, cooling and light people actually need. That is because electric technologies waste far less than fossil fuels. In the High Electrification Scenario, electricity reaches 35% of final energy by 2035 but supplies over half of all useful energy.

2) Transport has large potential. Battery prices have fallen 90% since 2010. Around half of oil-based road transport could be electrified competitively today. If battery costs keep falling, that rises to over four-fifths.

3) Heat pumps can compete in most places that need heat. They are competitive in around 75% of heating markets across advanced economies and China. Half of global space heating demand could be electrified cost-effectively.

4) Industry is the sleeping giant. Around 40% of energy used for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat can be electrified cost-effectively right now. More in the future.

5) Electrification is an energy security strategy. EVs already avoid 2.3 million barrels of oil a day. That is more than the volume that bypassed the Strait of Hormuz via the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline this summer. In the High Electrification Scenario, importers cut their fuel bills by USD 400 billion a year by 2035.

The gap is policy. Under current settings, electrification only reaches around 30% by 2035. Very few countries have a comprehensive, cross-sectoral electrification strategy. Grids need to expand 40% faster than over the past decade.

Before I led UNDP's work on decarbonization and sustainable energy, I served as Senior Principal Advisor for Small Island Developing States.
 
That work taught me something: in SIDS, energy is never just infrastructure. It's sovereignty. It's fiscal space. And after a storm, it's survival.
 
On Sept. 22, I'll be joining the AEG Caribbean Energy Roundtable during Climate Week. Here's what's on my mind:
 
Over 90% of energy across SIDS is imported oil. Caribbean households pay up to 3x more for electricity than in the US.
 
In Dominica, two primary schools destroyed by Hurricane Maria were rebuilt to survive Category 5 winds, with solar microgrids that now double as hurricane shelters. In Haiti, a 120-bed hospital in Bonne Fin with no grid connection ran straight through Hurricane Matthew on solar and batteries. 
 
Decentralization isn't the second-best option for small islands. It's the resilient one.
 
The region needs roughly $1.25B a year to transition.
But actual investment has been closer to $50M.
 
The technology isn't the gap. It's capital not showing up: 
- It's aging grids that can't absorb distributed generation. 
- It's projects stalling between preparation and financing. 
- And it's fiscal space: six of the world's ten most indebted small island economies are Caribbean, while fuel imports alone consume between 7 and 12% of GDP across much of the region, and over 20% in some.

Which is why I'm looking forward to this conversation. Not another round of pledges, but a room built to move money: leaders of Caribbean heritage alongside regional public, private, and civic partners, committed to catalytic impact within 12 months.
See you there. #ClimateWeekNYC #SIDS #EnergyTransition

public_card_text:
The global risk landscape has changed dramatically.

Yesterday, the 2026 United Nations Global Risk Report launched at an event hosted by Ambassador Burhan Gafoor, with keynote remarks from UN Under-Secretary-General Guy Ryder and a high-level discussion moderated by Ravi Agrawal , Editor-in-Chief of Foreign Policy .

One message stands out: the world’s perception of risk is shifting and the risk landscape has gotten more complex.

In the 2024 survey, concerns centered on environmental threats, misinformation, and pandemics. Just two years later, the map has been redrawn.

🔴 Geopolitics and conflict have moved to the center of global concern.
Large-scale war is now viewed as: 
• The most interconnected global risk
• The strongest driver of other risks
• One of the most important threats facing the world today

Most strikingly, it is no longer seen as a distant possibility. It recorded the single largest jump in perceived immediacy, climbing sixteen places in expectations of how soon it could materialize.

⚡ Technology risks are rising rapidly.
Respondents expressed significantly greater concern about AI and frontier technologies, as well as the concentration of power driven by technological change. At the same time, many believe global institutions are not adequately prepared to manage these risks, particularly given growing challenges around data, information, and governance.

🌍 Environmental risks remain fundamental.
Although attention has shifted toward geopolitical threats, climate change, natural hazards, and resource shortages continue to rank among the world's most important risks. These challenges have not disappeared. They now coexist with a growing set of political and technological pressures.

🤝 The risks may be changing. The solution is not.
Perhaps the most encouraging finding is this: across regions, sectors, and perspectives, respondents consistently identify joint action as the most effective response.

In a world where risks are increasingly interconnected and increasingly imminent, cooperation is not a luxury. It is a necessity.

The 2026 Global Risk Report is a timely reminder that while our threat landscape evolves, the need for collective action remains constant.

AI is creating a global race for power. Governments are moving quickly to build generation, grids and dedicated capacity for data centres. That urgency should extend to the energy needed by schools, hospitals, farms and businesses.

On 23 September, I will join the IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit during New York Climate Week to discuss The Role of AI in Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition.

The numbers show how quickly the energy landscape is changing:

Data-centre electricity consumption could almost double between 2025 and 2030, rising from around 485 TWh to 950 TWh.

More than 100 GW of new gas capacity is planned as dedicated onsite supply for data centres. Almost all of it is in the United States, with around 13 GW announced or under development elsewhere.

Middle-income countries generate around half of ChatGPT traffic, while low- and middle-income countries host only about one-quarter of global data-centre capacity.

AI is a double-edged sword for energy systems. It can improve renewable forecasting, grid management, efficiency and investment planning. It can also drive major new electricity demand, make fossil-fuel extraction cheaper and more productive, and extend dependence on existing fuels. Policies, safeguards and financing decisions will determine which effects dominate.

I look forward to discussing how countries can shape this expansion around their own development priorities: building additional clean power, strengthening grids, protecting people and ecosystems, and ensuring that the infrastructure and value created are more widely shared. #ClimateWeekNYC #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableAI

Could clean cooking be one of the most powerful opportunities to advance health, gender equality and sustainable development?
 
On the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, I keep coming back to clean cooking.
 
Nearly 2 billion people still lack access to clean cooking. In rural Sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of the population has access to clean cooking fuels.
 
The consequences reach far beyond the kitchen. Household air pollution caused an estimated 2.9 million deaths in 2021, while polluting cooking also affects productivity, gender equality and economic opportunity.
 
Yet the investment gap remains striking.
 
Around US$2.5 billion is invested in clean cooking solutions each year, less than a third of the US$8 billion needed annually to achieve universal access. Meanwhile, the health, environmental and productivity costs associated with polluting cooking are estimated at US$2.4–4 trillion every year.
 
For me, this makes clean cooking not simply an energy technology, but a development priority across the Global South.
 
Three shifts can help accelerate progress:
🔌 Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning. Nepal aims for 25% of households to adopt electric cooking by 2030, linking clean cooking directly to wider electrification efforts.
💰 Make finance reach the households most often left behind. Grants, subsidies and blended finance can help reduce upfront costs for rural and low-income communities.
🗺️ Use data and digital tools to target solutions better. Mapping grid reliability, consumer demand and e-cooking potential can help direct investment where it can deliver the greatest impact.
 
Clean air, energy access and development should not be treated as separate agendas.
 
Clean cooking can improve health, expand opportunity and make a just energy transition more inclusive at the same time. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #CleanCooking #CleanAir

⚡The energy transition is about Jobs. But where and for who ?
 
Renewable energy employment reached a record 16.6 million jobs globally in 2024.
 
Yet more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in just five countries and regions.
 
That raises a bigger question: the energy transition is creating enormous economic value — but who will have the opportunity to create, own and benefit from it?
 
A just transition is not only about creating more green jobs.
 
🏭 It is about socio-economic development, where new industries and supply chains are built. Between 2018 and 2024, China accounted for around 80% of global investment in manufacturing facilities for solar, wind, batteries and hydrogen technologies.
 
💰 It is about where investment flows. Low- and lower-middle-income countries are home to more than 40% of the world’s population, yet account for only 7% of global clean energy spending. In emerging and developing economies, the cost of capital for renewable energy projects can be two to three times higher than in advanced economies.
 
👷 It is about whether workers can access the opportunities being created. Around 60% of energy companies report labour shortages, and the number of graduates entering the energy sector would need to increase by around 40% by 2030 just to prevent today’s skills mismatch from worsening.
 
⚡ And it is about whether the transition ultimately delivers for people and planet. Even as clean energy investment and employment reach record levels, 655 million people worldwide still live without electricity.
 
These numbers are connected.
 
Where investment and manufacturing concentrate, jobs and economic value tend to follow.
 
For developing economies, a just transition must therefore be about more than replacing one energy source with another. It must help create decent jobs, build local industries and skills, expand affordable and reliable energy access, mobilize investment and support economic diversification.
 
As #UNGA81 gathers momentum, the question is not only how fast we can move. It is how we ensure more countries, communities and people can participate in creating the value generated by the transition — and share in its benefits.
 
Speed matters. But so does where the transition takes us — and who gets there with us. #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

⚡ What does development look like in an age when electricity is becoming more important to the global economy, but 655 million people still live without it?
 
As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opens today, the world is entering what the IEA calls the “Age of Electricity.”
 
🌍 92% of the world now has access to electricity. Yet 655 million people remain without it — and 86% of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
🍳 2 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
⚡ Meanwhile, global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6% annually through 2030, adding around 1,100 TWh each year.
 
💻 Data centres alone could consume around 945 TWh by 2030, more than double today’s level.
 
☀️ Renewables now provide over 30% of global electricity. But renewable generating capacity averages just 33.6 watts per person in low-income countries, compared with 1,224 watts in high-income countries — a gap of more than 36 times.
 
For me, these numbers point to a fundamental development challenge: we are building an increasingly electrified global economy, but we are not yet building it equally.
 
AI, data centres, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and cooling are increasing the value of reliable power. Yet where energy could unlock some of the greatest development gains, hundreds of millions still lack basic access.
 
The energy transition therefore cannot be measured only in gigawatts installed or emissions avoided. We also need to ask where new capacity is built, who can access it, and what opportunities it creates.
 
As leaders gather in New York, the opportunity is to make this “Age of Electricity” an age of development too — expanding access, creating jobs and investment, and enabling more countries to participate in the industries shaping the global economy.
 
The real measure of the energy transition will not only be how much energy we produce, but how widely its opportunities are shared. #UNGA81 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

⚡ Can the AI and energy revolutions grow without deepening water stress?
 
As World Water Week 2026 continues in Stockholm under the theme "Water for People and Progress," this is the question I keep coming back to: AI is no longer only an energy story.
 
By 2027, AI is projected to withdraw 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water annually, up to six times Denmark's total annual water withdrawal. Cooling is a major part of the equation. Data centres generate enormous amounts of heat, and removing that heat can require significant volumes of water, especially in hot climates.
 
I have come to see this as a siting and governance question rather than a technology one. Where digital infrastructure is built, and under what rules, will determine whether it strengthens or strains local water systems.
Three approaches are worth watching:
 
📐 Set measurable standards. Singapore's Green Data Center Roadmap prioritises energy efficiency and cooling technologies suited to tropical climates, and steers new development toward areas with cleaner grids and more abundant resources.
 
💧 Make water conditions part of approval. Malaysia, South-East Asia's most water-stressed country, has more than 100 proposed data centres that could consume over 808 million litres a day. Regulators now require all new facilities to use only recycled, reclaimed or rainwater as a condition of approval.
 
🌍 Plan for local conditions, not imported models. In Asia and the Pacific, water-use effectiveness averages 1.65 litres per kilowatt-hour, more than three times the global average of 0.5. Cooling strategies that work in Stockholm will not work in Kuala Lumpur.
 
For countries across the Global South, the opportunity is not simply to host the next generation of digital infrastructure, but to shape how it is powered, cooled and governed.
 
The AI revolution will be judged not only by what it computes, but by what it consumes. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #WorldWaterWeek

⚡ What if the path to universal energy access is not about choosing between grid and off-grid solutions, but planning them together?
 
That question is becoming more urgent. Electricity demand from data centres is set to more than double by 2030, reaching around 945 TWh. In several emerging data-centre hubs, AI infrastructure already accounts for 5 to 20 percent of total electricity demand.
For developing countries, digital growth can crowd in investment and modernise power systems, or compete with households, clinics and small businesses for limited electricity. The outcome depends on how power systems are planned today.
 
New analysis across Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria and Senegal shows why this matters. Where grid expansion is constrained, mini-grids can serve between 47 million and 110 million people out of 171 million needing access, accounting for more than half of new connections in some scenarios.
 
Battery storage can strengthen that pathway. Across the scenarios assessed, fuel savings average around US$2 for every US$1 of additional storage investment. Under optimistic mini-grid costs at Tier 2–3 demand levels, savings can reach up to US$4 for every US$1 invested by reducing diesel generation.
 
For me, the lesson is that grid extension, mini-grids, storage and digital infrastructure cannot be planned in isolation. Digital demand is reshaping power-system needs, while grids and storage determine how that growth can be served.
 
For countries still closing their access gaps, the opportunity is to plan grids, storage and digital growth together, so that rising demand expands access and opportunity rather than competing for scarce power.

⚡ Can the AI and energy revolutions grow without deepening water stress?
 
As World Water Week 2026 continues in Stockholm under the theme "Water for People and Progress," this is the question I keep coming back to: AI is no longer only an energy story.
 
By 2027, AI is projected to withdraw 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water annually, up to six times Denmark's total annual water withdrawal. Cooling is a major part of the equation. Data centres generate enormous amounts of heat, and removing that heat can require significant volumes of water, especially in hot climates.
 
I have come to see this as a siting and governance question rather than a technology one. Where digital infrastructure is built, and under what rules, will determine whether it strengthens or strains local water systems.
Three approaches are worth watching:
 
📐 Set measurable standards. Singapore's Green Data Center Roadmap prioritises energy efficiency and cooling technologies suited to tropical climates, and steers new development toward areas with cleaner grids and more abundant resources.
 
💧 Make water conditions part of approval. Malaysia, South-East Asia's most water-stressed country, has more than 100 proposed data centres that could consume over 808 million litres a day. Regulators now require all new facilities to use only recycled, reclaimed or rainwater as a condition of approval.
 
🌍 Plan for local conditions, not imported models. In Asia and the Pacific, water-use effectiveness averages 1.65 litres per kilowatt-hour, more than three times the global average of 0.5. Cooling strategies that work in Stockholm will not work in Kuala Lumpur.
 
For countries across the Global South, the opportunity is not simply to host the next generation of digital infrastructure, but to shape how it is powered, cooled and governed.
 
The AI revolution will be judged not only by what it computes, but by what it consumes. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #WorldWaterWeek

public_card_text:
“We’re not in an energy transition. We’re in an energy addition.” It’s a good line. And it has some serious people behind it who point out that fossil fuels still supply around 80% of global energy, barely down from 85% in 1990, while fossil demand keeps growing.

They have a point. Historically, clean energy has scaled too slowly to replace more fossil demand than the world adds each year. In absolute global primary energy terms, it looks like renewables have just been added on top.

But the argument draws the wrong conclusion, for two reasons.

First, global aggregates hide almost everything that matters. Look sectorally and regionally and you see systems already changing beyond recognition — EVs in Norway, batteries in California, solar in Pakistan, gas phasing down in Spain, heat pumps across the Nordics. Since 2016, clean energy has attracted more investment every year than fossil fuels, now roughly double. Around 90% of new power capacity is renewable. Nearly one in five cars sold worldwide is fully electric.

Second, and more fundamentally, the “80%” is based on a measurement error. It counts primary energy — but around two thirds of that is lost as waste heat in combustion before it delivers any useful service. Measuring the system this way inflates fossil fuels and understates both the efficiency of renewables and the demand we avoid through electrification. The share of useful energy (energy services) that clean energy provides is much larger than its share of primary energy consumption.

More in this week’s Bright Spots: https://lnkd.in/eP2Qe545

Power Beneath the Waves

The next frontier of renewable energy may not be in the sky. It may be beneath the ocean's surface.

Japan is accelerating the transition to clean energy by advancing underwater turbine technology that captures the immense power of ocean currents and tides. While solar panels rely on sunshine and wind turbines depend on weather, ocean currents are remarkably predictable, offering a reliable source of renewable electricity around the clock.

One of Japan's key milestones is the deployment of a 1.1 MW tidal turbine in the Naru Strait, alongside continued development of Kairyu, an innovative underwater turbine designed to harness the energy of the powerful Kuroshio Current. Together, these projects demonstrate how marine energy could become an important part of a diversified clean energy system.

The opportunity is significant.

🌊 Predictable power generation with minimal weather dependence.

⚡ Zero fuel consumption and near-zero operational emissions.

🔋 A valuable complement to solar and wind, helping improve grid stability.

🏝️ A sustainable energy solution for islands and coastal communities.

Yet challenges remain. Marine energy technologies must overcome high installation costs, harsh ocean conditions, maintenance complexity, and the need to protect marine ecosystems. Continued innovation and investment will determine how quickly these solutions become commercially competitive.

The energy transition will not be powered by a single technology. It will be built on a portfolio of solutions—solar, wind, geothermal, hydropower, energy storage, and increasingly, the vast and largely untapped energy flowing through our oceans.

The future of clean energy isn't just above us. It's all around us—including beneath the waves. #RenewableEnergy #OceanEnergy #TidalEnergy #CleanEnergy #EnergyTransition #ClimateInnovation #Sustainability #NetZero

In 2019, Ghana launched the Year of Return, a nationwide campaign commemorating 400 years since the first enslaved Africans were taken from its shores. Backed by a $3.5 million investment, the initiative encouraged Africans in the diaspora to reconnect with their heritage through festivals, cultural events, and visits to historic sites such as Cape Coast Castle. The campaign attracted global figures including Idris Elba, Naomi Campbell , and Steve Harvey , while visitor arrivals surged 45%, average tourist spending increased from $1,862 to $2,589, and tourism generated an estimated $1.9 billion for the Ghanaian economy.

Rather than ending after one year, Ghana expanded the initiative into Beyond the Return, a 10-year program running through 2030 aimed at strengthening long-term ties with the African diaspora. The country also reinforced its commitment through policies allowing people of African descent in the Americas to reside indefinitely in Ghana. Since then, citizenship ceremonies have accelerated, with around 1,500 people choosing to permanently relocate, while diaspora buyers now account for nearly 30% of high-end property purchases in Accra.

Ghana's approach demonstrates how cultural heritage can be transformed into a long-term economic strategy. By using tourism as an entry point to encourage citizenship, real estate investment, and entrepreneurship, the country has positioned itself as a leading destination for the African diaspora seeking to reconnect with the continent. The success of the initiative has also inspired broader conversations across Africa about attracting diaspora talent, investment, and expertise to support the continent's development.

⚡ Renewables can do more than generate clean power. Combined with modern grids, storage and digital intelligence, they can deliver reliable energy for people.
 
In 2025, the world added a record 692 GW of renewable power capacity, alongside 108 GW of new battery storage, 40% more than the year before.

For close to 1 billion people served by health facilities with unreliable electricity or none at all, reliability determines whether vaccines stay cold, medical equipment works and essential care continues.  
 
Three investments can unlock this opportunity:
 
🌍 Modern and decentralized grids bring clean energy closer to people, connecting generation, storage and demand while helping essential services withstand disruptions.
 
🔋 Storage makes variable power dependable, capturing electricity when supply is abundant and releasing it when demand rises.
 
📊 Digital management adds flexibility. Better forecasting and digitally enabled demand response could reduce renewable curtailment by more than 25% by 2030.
 
Across the Global South, this is an opportunity to build renewable capacity and the infrastructure that makes it reliable at the same time.
 
Renewable capacity shows what we can generate. Integrated energy systems show what we can deliver. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyStorage #EnergyResilience

What does my mother's couscous teaches us about industrial policy? 

Well, a lot, as it turns out! My mother, Fatima, is like the East Asian 'miracle'. You can try to copy her recipes, but you will probably will not get the same results. It turns out that what make her cuisine brilliant is that she can easily adapt and change it based on the ingredients and ustentils she has access to. She has never shared a recipe without explaining "if you have X, do Y. If not, do Z". And for industrial policy, it is the same: success is not defined by the quality of policy instrument or budgets, as much as the capacity of the cook to adapt and change the recipe based on changing conditions and institutional constraints. What is also means is that industrial policy is a living dynamic system that needs to constantly learning and adjust, not a blueprint. 

I am glad this piece (drawn from recent research for UNU-WIDER - United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research is part of the 50-year anniversary book of the The OPEC Fund for International Development . What does it mean for the energy transition to reach the grid, the data centre and the electric vehicle, but still not reach the kitchen?
 
Today’s discussion brought that challenge into focus at the 2026 HLPF Regional Satellite Event, “From Commitment to Implementation: A Regional Dialogue on Coordinated UN-Energy Action for Clean Cooking.”
 
Clean cooking remains one of the most urgent and overlooked development challenges. While the world is investing over US$2.2 trillion in the energy transition, 2 billion people still cook with polluting fuels, and 1.8 billion are projected to remain without clean cooking in 2030.
 
The discussions made clear that clean cooking sits at the heart of health, gender equality, climate action and human dignity. Household air pollution caused 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including 309,000 children under five, while women and girls continue to carry the burden of smoke exposure and fuel collection.
 
Yet progress is possible: since 2010, India, China and Indonesia have driven 80% of the global reduction in the clean cooking access gap.
 
The conversation also reinforced the need for smarter, more targeted delivery. Of the 2 billion people without clean cooking access, 1.5 billion live in rural areas, and the top 20 access-deficit countries account for around three-quarters of the global gap. Using geospatial analytics and AI-driven tools such as the Clean Energy Equity Index, UNDP helps countries identify underserved communities and target clean energy investments where they are needed most.
 
But delivery also needs finance and systems that can turn commitments into results. Universal clean cooking access requires around US$8 billion annually, while the cost of inaction is estimated at US$2.4 trillion each year. Examples from Ghana, Rwanda and Morocco show how clear targets, public finance and delivery systems can move clean cooking from pledge to practice.
 
I left the discussion with one clear reflection: the energy transition cannot be judged only by how much power we generate, but by whether it reaches the kitchens, classrooms, clinics and communities still being left behind. #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #CleanCooking #CleanEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #UNEnergy #UNDP

Across our world, natural resources are dramatically altering the causes, dynamics, and outcomes of conflict.

Critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements are gaining in strategic importance. Surging global demand creates opportunities for development, but it is also driving geopolitical competition, straining supply chains, and fuelling conflict with dire humanitarian consequences.

Too often, revenues from the illicit exploitation of natural resources strengthen armed and criminal actors, connect local violence to regional and international networks, and weaken incentives for political compromise.

The challenge is to transform how natural resources are extracted, processed, brought to market, and used - ensuring more added value is retained by producing countries and affected communities.

Natural resources must be managed to finance inclusive and sustainable development, strengthen institutions, and advance peace and prosperity for all.

No more exploitation. No more plundering.

US$2 trillion was invested in clean energy globally last year, yet international public clean energy finance for developing countries amounted to just US$24.6 billion.
 
At today's Building Investment Plans to Unlock Climate Finance for Vulnerable Nations dialogue at #HLPF2026 , I posed a simple question: Are SIDS and LDCs truly lacking bankable projects, or are we failing to recognize where value is being created?
 
The economics of the energy transition are increasingly compelling. Renewable electricity costs are projected to fall 30% by 2030, while electricity demand over the next five years is expected to grow 50% faster than over the previous decade. Capital is available. Demand is growing.
 
The opportunity is to connect the two.
 
That starts with better data. UNDP's satellite analysis identified 1.18 billion people living in energy poverty, around 60% more than those captured by conventional electricity access metrics. Better intelligence helps reveal hidden demand, reduce investment risk, and direct finance where it can deliver the greatest development impact.
 
It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31. #EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #PreCOP31 #RisingUpForSIDS

In 1949, the world was home to 2.2 billion people. Today, we are more than 8.2 billion. Every week, the world's population grows by roughly 1.3 million people—equivalent to adding a city the size of Prague every seven days. Almost all of that growth is taking place in developing economies. By 2050, these countries are expected to account for around 85% of global energy demand growth. 

The future of the energy transition will therefore be shaped where populations, cities and industries are expanding the fastest.
These demographic trends are reshaping the geography of development, investment and opportunity.

I was pleased to contribute to the discussion during the #HLPF last week "From Vulnerability to Investment: Overcoming Barriers to Energy Access, Resilient Infrastructure and Green Industrialization in LDCs," co-organized by Nepal, the State of Qatar, UN-OHRLLS and UNIDO.

A just energy transition should not be seen only as a pathway to decarbonization, but as a vehicle to strengthen energy security, build economic resilience, and preserve the natural systems on which future development depends.

Countries such as Bhutan and Nepal demonstrate what is possible. In Bhutan, hydropower has become a pillar of economic development and exports. In Nepal, more than 400 community micro-hydro systems have provided electricity to over 500,000 people while supporting more than 1,000 rural enterprises. Energy has created businesses, incomes and opportunities—not just electricity connections.Those examples show the importance of creating the right conditions for investment. 

Expanding domestic renewable energy can reduce exposure to volatile fuel imports—where a 50% increase in oil prices could add around US$16 billion to LDC import bills. Regional power markets can unlock larger investment opportunities, while better de-risking and blended finance can mobilize private capital where financing costs remain the main barrier. 

In The Gambia, a UNDP-supported mini-grid commissioned this year supplies electricity to 375 households and more than 75 small businesses—from welders and tailors to cold storage—demonstrating how energy access can become an investable local economy. In Zambia, the national electrification agency is co-financing a new electrification programme with an investment nearly ten times larger than the UNDP-managed grant, illustrating how catalytic finance can mobilize domestic resources and scale impact.

The impact of a just energy transition should ultimately be measured not only by the number of people connected, but by the jobs it creates, the resilience it builds, the nature it preserves, and the economic opportunities it unlocks. HLPF 2026: SDG7 had its stocktake. Now the final four years have to prove what access actually enables.

One week on from the HLPF review of #SDG7 , the outcome gave energy the political weight it deserves. It treated SDG7 not just as an energy target, but as a test of whether sustainable development can still deliver by 2030. The remaining gap will not be closed by ambition alone; it’ll be closed through the practical choices now made on access, clean cooking, grids, storage, finance, partnerships and women’s leadership.

But the data cut through that language…

…Because the reality is that global electricity access has stalled at 92%, while ~1.18 billion people remain energy poor, including ~447 million who are officially connected but still unable to use electricity meaningfully... That is the SDG7 blind spot for the final four years: access on paper is not the same as affordable, reliable power that supports productive use, resilience and dignity.📣‼️

Time will tell whether this stocktake becomes a turning point for delivery; not just stronger language, but a different test of what access enables, who benefits and who remains outside the system:

1️⃣ Access has to be judged by what it enables. A connection is not the finish line. SDG7 has to mean affordability, reliability, clean cooking, productive use, resilience, livelihoods and dignity.

2️⃣ Delivery has to connect the systems around energy. Finance, grids, skills, industrial strategy, digital demand and labour markets cannot keep moving as separate conversations. That is where implementation either scales or fails.

3️⃣ Data has to expose the gaps that averages hide. If this transition is meant to be just, gender-responsive and intergenerationally inclusive, then we need to know who benefits, who leads, who carries the burden and who remains invisible.

That is the real test after this stocktake: whether SDG7 can move from progress language into delivery systems that reach the people and places still outside them. #EnergyKiltMan #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #JustTransition #EnergyAccess

"The clean energy transition is unstoppable. The question is whether the development transition will keep pace."
 
That was the defining message emerging from the UN High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals and the thematic roundtables at #HLPF2026 .
 
Demand for critical energy transition minerals is expected to almost triple by 2030, while around US$500 billion in new mining investment will be needed by 2040. Yet between 2020 and 2024, nearly 90 percent of new refining capacity for key critical minerals was added by a single leading producer for each mineral. The challenge is no longer only securing supply. It is creating more diversified, resilient and equitable value chains that also deliver development.
 
Throughout yesterday’s  discussions, one message resonated across governments, industry, international organizations, Indigenous Peoples and civil society:
The energy transition cannot repeat yesterday's extractive model.
 
Resource-rich countries should not remain exporters of raw materials while higher-value industries, technology and jobs are created elsewhere. Critical minerals must become a catalyst for industrialization, economic diversification, decent work and long-term prosperity.
 
The conversation has moved beyond principles. It is now about implementation. 
 
The Secretary-General's Guiding Principles provide the roadmap. The task now is to translate them into country-level action through stronger institutions, financing, technology transfer, local value creation and trusted international partnerships.
 
As co-chair of the UN Joint Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, together with UNCTAD and UNEP, and with UNDP leading the Country Support Mechanism, we are working with countries to turn these principles into practical support that strengthens governance, mobilizes investment and helps countries move up mineral value chains.
 
Critical minerals can power the energy transition if we ensure they also power development. #EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #UNDP

Can AI become a catalyst for sustainable development without becoming a growing burden on the planet?

That was the central question from today’s 2026 HLPF side event on Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation. As the HLPF draws to a close, the discussion reinforced that digital transformation must be integrated into the sustainable development agenda.

AI is reshaping development, but behind every algorithm lies a physical system powered by electricity, water, minerals and infrastructure. By 2030, data centres could use 945 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent of the current electricity consumption of Africa.

By 2030, AI is expected to add US$15.7 trillion to the global economy, while developing countries may capture only 10% of that value.

I shared insights from UNDP ’s report, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries, which shows that AI’s next frontier will depend as much on energy systems as computing power. It calls for Green AI that advances people, protects the planet and expands prosperity by aligning digital investment with clean energy and national priorities.

I shared three key priorities: directing AI towards practical development challenges, building skills and innovation ecosystems that create domestic value, and embedding sustainability and accountability into investment from the outset.

Examples are emerging. In Kenya, AI-enabled energy systems are improving affordability and resilience. In Moldova, UNDP is supporting 500,000 smart meters by 2030. UNDP tools, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index and the Electricity Access Forecasting Model, are helping countries improve AI and digital planning and resilience.

My takeaway is that the Global Digital Compact must move from ambition to implementation. Beyond 2030, digital progress should be defined not by technological scale alone, but by its contribution to inclusion, resilience and sustainable development. #UNDP #HLPF2026 #GreenAI #DigitalSustainability

The cheapest tariff can still produce the highest energy cost.
Reliability decides what electricity really costs on site.

The visual shows a useful comparison of residential electricity tariffs 
across 22 African markets.

Same benchmark:

100 kWh per month.
Low-voltage household band.
Volumetric charge only.

The spread is huge.

Sierra Leone sits at 
22.8 cents per kWh.

Ethiopia sits at 
1.3 cents.

At first glance, this looks like a price story.

The real story sits underneath it.

A low tariff can come from 

cheap hydro.

It can also come from 

subsidies, 
weak cost recovery, 
underfunded utilities 
grids struggling to maintain themselves.

A high tariff can reflect 

diesel exposure, 
fuel imports, 
small grid scale, 
island economics
limited generation diversity.

Then reliability changes the calculation.

A low-tariff kilowatt hour gets
expensive when the site 
still needs 

Diesel.
Batteries.
Inverters.
Spare parts.
Maintenance.
Downtime cover.

For a factory, mine, hospital, 
cold-chain facility or telecom site, 
the tariff is only the visible layer.

The operating cost sits below it.

The better questions are:

Is the tariff cost-reflective?

What is the C&I price?
How reliable is the grid?
How much subsidy is hidden?
How much backup power is still required?
How does purchasing power change the ranking?

For African power users, the real energy question goes beyond price.

Affordable power matters.
Reliable power matters.
Bankable power matters.

The tariff sits on the bill.

The real cost shows up in the operation.

As many wait patiently for tonight's #WorldCup verdict, Amir Lebdioui and I have just released a Substack post to help make the wait less painful.

Against the idea that success in football is just a story of culture or generational luck, we argue it's better understood as just another sector where competitiveness is deliberately built through strategic policy-making.

Football talent development, it turns out, closely resembles another long-term planning policy at the heart of many debates today: industrial policy.

As such, many of industrial policy's key questions—how to pick winners under uncertainty, how to build a competitive ecosystem rather than a single champion, when to rely on foreign expertise versus building your own—can be thought about through football. #Football should never lose its magic. But most of the teams that keep showing up, tournament after tournament, or those that emerge as new challengers, are the ones that stopped waiting for magic and started treating football as a strategic sector.

The race for critical energy transition minerals will shape not only the future of clean energy—it will shape the future of development, industrialization and geopolitics.

The question is whether resource-rich developing countries will simply supply the raw materials for the energy transition—or become full participants in the industries and prosperity that it creates.

That was the focus of this week’s first United Nations  High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals and the subsequent meeting of the UN Task Force, marking an important transition from principles to implementation.

Building on the Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals—which received strong support from Member States—we are now focused on turning its Guiding Principles and Recommendations into action.

One message came through loud and clear:

The clean energy transition must not repeat the mistakes of the past.

Countries endowed with critical mineral resources want more than extraction. They want to create value at home through processing, manufacturing, industrialization, skills development, quality jobs and sustainable investment. They want their mineral wealth to become a foundation for long-term prosperity.

Another message was equally powerful.

No government can achieve this alone.

Building resilient, responsible and equitable mineral value chains requires governments, industry, investors, Indigenous Peoples, workers, local communities, civil society, development finance institutions and international organizations working together.

This is where the United Nations has a unique role to play.

Through the UN Task Force and its Country Support Mechanism, more than 20 UN entities and international organizations are joining forces to help countries strengthen governance, mobilize investment, develop value-addition strategies, build institutional capacity and ensure that critical energy transition minerals become a driver of sustainable development.

At a time of growing geopolitical competition, this agenda demonstrates that international cooperation remains indispensable.

The race for critical minerals must not become a race to the bottom. It must become a race to create more value, more opportunity and more shared prosperity.

That is the vision that brought governments together this week. Now comes the harder—and more important—task: delivering results on the ground.

My sincere thanks to all Member States and to our colleagues across UNDP, UN Environment Programme , UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) , United Nations Development Coordination Office (UNDCO), UNIDO,  the UN Regional Commissions, and The World Bank Group  for their leadership and collaboration as we move from vision to implementation.

#CriticalMinerals #EnergyTransition #ClimateAction #SustainableDevelopment #Industrialization #JustTransition #UnitedNations

Institutional engagement should always be a key part of our engineering journey. While we are very much focused on technological advancements, there is a significant human element that relates to implementation. While looking forward to presenting at the IEEE Power & Energy Society general meeting this week, I made a pit stop in New York. While I had no plans to attend the High-Level Political Forum, it was a lucky coincidence to be in New York during the post-HLPF days and to meet with the UNDP New York team on decarbonization and energy, led by  Riad Meddeb, alongside Stefano Pistolese Hitomi Yamaguchi, who have always been a close family. 

In today's engagements, UNDP contributed to the HLPF side event "Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation: Aligning the Global Digital Compact". They highlighted its latest publication, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race, which explores how countries can align AI, energy, infrastructure, skills, and natural resources to capture the opportunities of the digital transition. Discussions were focused on AI, Digital Public Infrastructure, and other innovations can accelerate the SDGs while managing their environmental footprint, and how the Global Digital Compact can support a more sustainable Beyond 2030 agenda.

The on-ground reality is that the way infrastructure needs assessments are conducted is changing rapidly. The last decades' projected infrastructure transformation is no longer applicable in many locations across the world. Concepts such as "large loads" are coming to the center of the conversation. These large loads (such as AI data centers, semiconductor fabs, hydrogen production facilities, electric vehicle charging hubs, and large industrial electrification projects) require a different type of grid infrastructure because their electricity demand is much greater, more concentrated, faster-growing, and sometimes more sensitive than traditional loads. While these advancements are related, changes are discussed in the technology spaces, the interlinkage to the development space is vital. Which is one of the reasons we stay close to the multilateral system while supporting the advancements in technolgy. 

Shay Bahramirad - Ph.D. Riad Meddeb UNDP United Nations #hlpf #unga #undp #infrastructure #codes #digitalcompact

Earlier this year, becoming a mother made me look at everyday technology from a different perspective.

Living in Türkiye, where we enjoy around 2,640–2,741 hours of sunshine each year (roughly 7.2–7.5 hours a day), it is easy to recognize the country's enormous solar potential, not only in large infrastructure projects but also in the technologies we use every day. 

One of the things we bought for our home was a camera with a solar panel. It was a small choice that made me reflect on Türkiye's remarkable solar energy growth.

In just over a decade, Türkiye's installed solar capacity has grown from 40.2 MW in 2014 to 25,827 MW by January 2026—a 641-fold increase. Solar's share of installed electricity capacity has risen from 0.1% to 20.9%, meaning 1 in every 5 megawatts of installed capacity now comes from solar.

The progress is equally remarkable in electricity generation, which increased from just 17 GWh in 2014 to 38,069 GWh by the end of 2025.

Looking ahead, Türkiye aims to reach 120 GW of installed wind and solar capacity by 2035, requiring annual additions of 8-10 GW.

This year, Türkiye will host COP31. One of the Presidency's key objectives is to increase global electrification to 35% by 2035, recognizing the critical role of clean electricity in decarbonizing economies and expanding energy access.

The energy transition matters at every level - from the technologies we choose for our homes to national renewable energy strategies and the global conversations that shape climate action. #COP31 #Türkiye #EnergyTransition #SolarEnergy UNDP in Europe and Central Asia COP31 Türkiye Brief UNDP

public_card_text:
72% of electricity meters in Great Britain are smart meters.

In Germany, it's just 5.5%.

That gap isn't really about technology. It's about public policy — and it says a lot about how ready each country is for what comes next.

Britain treated smart meters as essential infrastructure:
→ National deployment targets
→ Regulatory obligations on utilities
→ Investment in a shared digital communications network

Germany treated them as a consumer product:
→ Narrower deployment requirements
→ Heavier emphasis on privacy and cybersecurity
→ Costs left largely to households

The result isn't just a slower rollout in Germany. It's a different capacity to support the next phase of electrification.

Here's why that matters:

Smart meters are the gateway to the new electricity economy. Without one, you can't access variable tariffs that reward you for using power when renewables are abundant. You can't optimise solar, batteries or heat pumps. You can't take part in flexibility markets or bidirectional EV charging.

The lesson goes well beyond meters.

Countries that treat digitally enabled electricity systems as strategic national infrastructure — not optional consumer upgrades — will move faster on clean energy, energy security, and competitiveness.

Just as past generations invested collectively in roads, railways and broadband, this generation needs to invest in intelligent electricity networks.

The hardest part of this isn't technological. It's financial.

If households are left to fund this transformation mainly through higher bills, the transition will be slower, less fair, and politically harder to sustain.

Governments, regulators, utilities and capital markets should instead treat this as productive public investment — shifting the upfront cost away from households and toward long-term infrastructure financing.

Electrification is about far more than replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy.

It's about building the infrastructure for a digitally enabled, clean energy system — bringing together the two most powerful drivers of innovation and competitiveness in the twenty-first century: the green transition and the digital revolution. #Electrification #EnergyTransition #EnergySecurity #CleanEnergy #DigitalInfrastructure #Energiewende #Verkehrswende

public_card_text:
Ten years ago, one in every 100 cars sold worldwide was electric. Last year, it was one in four. That is one of the fastest technology transitions in the history of energy.

But what is the real meaning of mobility?

It is more than moving people—it is about connecting them to opportunity. Today, less than half of the world's population has access to public transport, and in many developing cities fewer than half of jobs can be reached within one hour. Mobility expands access to jobs, education and healthcare, strengthening social cohesion by connecting communities and national cohesion by linking regions, reducing inequalities and expanding economic opportunity.

E-mobility is therefore about more than replacing fuel cars with electric ones. If we're redesigning how we move, why not redesign the spaces we move through? In many cities, roads and parking already occupy up to 30–40% of urban land—space that could instead support people, nature and more resilient communities.

Imagine cities with fewer parking lots, wider sidewalks, more bus lanes, green corridors, urban forests and vibrant public spaces. The energy transition is also an opportunity to rethink the built environment itself. Electrification should be the starting point for cities built around people—not simply an electric version of today's car-centric model. In the Global South, where most future urban growth will occur, this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to build cities differently.

Yesterday, at the HLPF side event on Advancing the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026–2035), I had the opportunity to discuss these ideas organized by Global Sustainable Transport Innovation and Knowledge Center and UNDESA.

The momentum is encouraging: EV sales in emerging economies outside China grew by around 80% in 2025, while the global EV fleet is now displacing around 1.7 million barrels of oil demand every day.

In Sri Lanka, UNDP is supporting the transition of 500,000 tuk-tuks to electric vehicles over five years—reducing fuel imports while creating new opportunities for drivers, women and vulnerable groups.

These models work because they fit local economies. They are becoming even more viable because battery pack costs have fallen by 93% since 2010.

It means recognizing that, in many countries, two- and three-wheelers may deliver the greatest development impact. It means using data and digitalization to enable smart charging and vehicle-to-grid integration, embedding e-mobility within national energy planning, accelerating public transport electrification, and creating more value in the countries where the critical minerals powering this transition are sourced.

If the future is electric, shouldn't we also redesign the spaces we move through? #UNDP #HLPF2026 #EMobility #SustainableTransport #EnergyTransition Riad Meddeb , Xie Hui , Elif Su Duygun , Tamara Rasamny تمارا الرسامني, Clement Amponsah , Hitomi Yamaguchi

public_card_text:
Can we truly call an energy system sustainable if it eventually becomes a waste system?

This thought-provoking question was posed by Mr Riad Meddeb, Head of Decarbonization and Sustainable Energy at UNDP, during the #HLPF2026 side event: "Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa"

Held at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, the session was co-organised by Circular Economy Powered Renewable Energy Centre - CEPREC, Chatham House, UNDP, Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE), African Circular Economy Alliance (ACEA), African Development Bank Group and De Montfort University.

The session brought together Member State representatives, UN agencies, regional bodies, researchers, development partners and civil society actors to examine how circular renewable energy systems can support Africa’s clean energy transition.

The discussion moved beyond renewable energy deployment alone. It asked a deeper question: how can Africa expand energy access while avoiding future waste, dependency, affordability challenges and missed opportunities for local value creation?

The session was chaired by Professor Muyiwa Oyinlola, CEPREC Director and Professor of Innovation for Sustainable Development at De Montfort University, with opening framing from Mr Riad Meddeb of UNDP. It featured contributions from representatives of the Permanent Missions of South Africa, Sierra Leone, China and Nigeria to the United Nations, the African Circular Economy Alliance (ACEA), Chatham House Environment and Society, University of Warwick - Warwick Business School, the University of Lagos, ENERGIA Network, UNDP Planet Hub, the SDG7 Youth Constituency, and other partners working across energy, circular economy, policy and implementation.

Key themes included circular design, local value chains for repair and reuse, second-life batteries, standards and e-waste governance, digital tools for transparency and trust, lifecycle finance, and stronger participation by women, young people, informal workers and local enterprises.

The conversation also highlighted the importance of connecting SDG 7 with SDG 8, SDG 9, SDG 11, SDG 12, SDG 13 and SDG 17, while aligning circular renewable energy systems with Africa’s longer-term development vision under Agenda 2063.

For CEPREC, the discussion speaks directly to our mission: generating evidence, building capacity and supporting implementation pathways for circular renewable energy systems across Africa.

Africa’s energy transition must not only deploy more renewable technologies.

It must create systems that deliver access, resilience, jobs, inclusion, local value creation and long-term sustainability.

Thank you to all speakers, partners and participants who contributed to such a rich and timely discussion.

#CEPREC #CircularRenewableEnergy #CircularMicrogrids #HLPF2026 #SDG7

Ahead of next week's High-Level Political Forum, the latest Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report offers an important snapshot of where the global energy transition stands—and why this may be one of the greatest development opportunities of our time.
 
The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.
Today, investing in clean energy is no longer driven only by climate ambition. It is increasingly about energy security, economic competitiveness, industrial development and resilience.
 
At the same time, digitalization and AI are creating new opportunities to build smarter grids, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewables and expand access to affordable and reliable energy.
 
Accelerating renewable energy deployment and energy efficiency strengthens energy security, reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and enhances macroeconomic resilience, particularly in developing countries.
Important gaps remain. 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030, nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels, and globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford a basic electricity connection.
 
Universal access will require us to more than triple the current pace of progress.
 
As the final in-depth review of SDG 7 before 2030, this year's High-Level Political Forum is an opportunity not only to assess progress, but to redefine the just energy transition as one of the strongest drivers of development, resilience, prosperity and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.
 
Read the updated SDG7 Tracker Report here: https://lnkd.in/esBEd7AV

In 2024, 655 million people were still living without access to electricity, and 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030. Nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting fuels for cooking, while globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford the monthly cost of a basic electricity service.
 
These figures, presented in the latest SDG 7 Tracking Report, remind us why a just energy transition matters. It is about far more than turning on the lights. Clean, affordable, and reliable energy has the power to transform societies—expanding opportunities for education, healthcare, jobs, and economic development, while strengthening resilience and turning today's uncertainties into tomorrow's opportunities.
 
At the same time, the global energy landscape is becoming increasingly complex. Rising geopolitical tensions are exposing vulnerabilities in energy systems and supply chains, while the rapid expansion of AI is driving an unprecedented surge in electricity demand, with data centres projected to consume more electricity by 2030 than all but the world's five largest electricity-consuming countries.
 
How do we accelerate progress towards SDG 7 in a world of rising energy demand, digital transformation, and widening financing gaps? More importantly, what practical solutions and emerging opportunities can help us get back on track?

Together with colleagues from across the UN system, we will discuss the latest SDG 7 findings, explore practical solutions and emerging opportunities, and examine how to accelerate implementation by advancing energy access, mobilising finance, and strengthening the links between energy, industrial development, and digital transformation.

SDG7 isn’t just about who gets connected. It's about what energy makes possible.📣

Contributing to the review of this year’s Tracking SDG7 Progress Report through the SDG7 Youth Constituency of the Major Group for Children and Youth made one thing impossible to ignore:

👉 Energy access only matters if it changes what people are able to do👈

And the latest data gives us a clear reality check: progress is visible, but still far too uneven.

The priority now has to be meaningful delivery.

Three areas stand out:

1️⃣ Energy access must mean outcomes, not connections alone. Electricity access has stalled at 92%, with 655 million people still without electricity in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for 563 million of that total, while many newly connected households still face unreliable, unaffordable or poor-quality service.

2️⃣ Clean cooking must sit at the centre of SDG7 delivery. Around 2.0 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. Without a course correction, 1.8 billion people could still lack clean cooking access by 2030.

3️⃣ Finance must reach where energy poverty is concentrated. Public clean energy flows reached at least USD 24.6 billion in 2024, but flows to LDCs fell by 11%. LDCs, LLDCs and SIDS collectively received less than 30% of public clean energy finance, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the global population without electricity access.

These aren’t just access gaps. They’re development gaps; shaping whether people can study, work, access healthcare, build businesses and live with dignity.

What’s missing isn’t technology. It’s the urgency, coordination and political will to match commitments with resources AND to make sure progress translates into delivery on the ground.

⚽ Tenuous football hook, as 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 England are warming-up for their first #WorldCup match...

Our #DigitalEnergyStack is a lot like a football team. If one position is weak, then the whole potential (or team) is constrained.

The Digital Energy Stack is one way in which we're working with governments to put all of the tech and non-tech pieces into play, and supporting them in benefitting from the twin revolutions of AI and clean energy. We have:

1️⃣ Data, 2️⃣ Connectivity, and 3️⃣ Compute - the defence. The robust and dependable foundations that drive digital and energy impact.

4️⃣ Digital Public Infrastructure - the midfielders, and the 'engine room' of inclusive energy access. The core tech components that increase the reach and impact of our sustainable energy efforts.

5️⃣ Cybersecurity - the goalkeeper (stretching this now...). Digital is increasingly becoming a first line of national defence, but is also presenting security concerns for critical national infrastructure such as energy.

And then we have 6️⃣ AI. Perhaps the striker? High-profile, speedy, and about impact (goals). And reliant on the rest of the #stack . AI is already driving increased energy uptake, improving grid planning, and strengthening energy inclusion. Particularly as digital and data foundations deepen. 

And, finally(!) 7️⃣ governance. Digital and energy impact is not about technology, but about people. Building the skills, expertise, leadership, and culture to explore, embrace, and embed innovation in energy. This is our team manager 🧢. Joining everything together, and making the impact greater than the sum of its parts.

Read more in our illuminem piece: https://lnkd.in/eZKHj2rF Curious to hear how digital is fitting into your energy work Riad Meddeb , Amir Lebdioui , Josh Oxby , Waldemar Koehler , Toyo Kawabata, PhD , Andrea Renzulli , Jacqueline L. , Syed Ahmed , Matt Clifton, Daniela Protas , Per Christer Lund , Gareth Walsh , Jeremy Yapp , Piyush Verma , Carlos Salgado , Jordan Lee , Marcus Saul , Julia Heinz, Karim Elgendy , Yann Grynberg , Andrea Gori , Francesca Battaglia Trovato .

public_card_text:
Everyone is talking about the AI 'race'. But races aren't won in the first corner. They're won in the final sprint - and over the very last mile. And the last mile is something that the Global South knows very well.

Far from being left out or left behind, the Global South could set the pace for global AI direction. And we're working with governments around the world to prepare them for what we see as the crucial AI 'sprint' - in particular, how countries can position energy and AI as crucial catalysts for growth. With these two revolutions having the potential to become definitive inflection points for 21st century sustainable development. 

We've identified a 'Green Window of Opportunity' where decision-makers, policymakers, and innovators can leverage the combined potential of energy and AI to chart a new pathway. Some of the areas we're driving exploration around include:

🤝 How to build locally-owned and locally-relevant domestic AI–energy innovation ecosystems anchored in local talent, universities, businesses, and public institutions.

🏛️ The need to make 'Green AI' THE critical pathway through supportive regulation, infrastructure planning, and investment incentives - with the potential for this to become an area of national comparative advantage.

⬆️ Identifying how countries and communities can move up the clean energy, critical mineral, and digital value chains to retain greater economic value domestically - and how they can build crucial and cumulative energy, AI, and development gains.

⚡ How countries can shape and support AI and clean-energy entrepreneurs through targeted finance, incubation, market creation, and skills development.

We are not about abstract discussions of technology, status quo energy policy, or generic policy recommendations. We really do see an important moment for development in the coming months and years. Countries sitting at the intersection of renewable energy - many of which are in the Global South - and AI explorations (with countries across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific moving quickly) could reap an unprecedented digital development dividend. Get in touch if you want to explore what the AI and energy revolutions could mean for your country.

➡️ More in our recent UNDP  paper with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford : The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries?

Sustainable and inclusive energy access is a literal catalyst to all 1️⃣7️⃣ SDGs. But how can we make it happen? We're proposing a holistic and systems-level approach to leveraging tech to drive a just energy transition. We call it the 'Digital Energy Stack' ⬇️

The ‘digital energy stack’ is 7️⃣ tech (and non-tech) components that countries need to engage with to maximise the benefits of the AI, digital, and energy revolutions. 

📊 Data: the fuel of the energy revolution. From the Big Data generated by smart meters to the ‘Thick’ Data that needs to inform service design and policymaking.

📱 Connectivity: the wired and wireless infrastructure that lets data flow between energy solutions and stakeholders – and drives energy business models. 

🌐 Compute: the ‘currency’ of the 21st century - creating opportunities for improved energy planning and delivery, but also challenges of energy and resource use.

🛣️ Digital Public Infrastructure: the ‘roads and railways’ of our digital economies and societies, DPI could deepen the impact of digital energy solutions. 

🔒 Cybersecurity: energy is critical national infrastructure. It needs to be ‘resilient-by-design’ and we need energy professionals with cyber skills.

🤖 AI: already having an impact - whether in improving energy planning or driving new approaches for credit-scoring that make energy services more accessible.

🏛️ Governance: how we shape the skills, expertise, processes, institutions, and organisational cultures – within and beyond government – to truly engage with the potential that digital offers for energy.
