Even as renewable investments surge globally, now exceeding USD 1.8 trillion annually and outpacing fossil fuels two-to-one, overall energy investment across Eurasia has fallen by nearly 30% since 2015.
 
Yet the region holds vast untapped potential. Regional cooperation is already reshaping its energy future, such as the recent MoU between Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan to advance the Caspian Green Energy Corridor, creating a new axis for renewable power trade, jobs, and local value chains.
 
This region will be the backdrop for this year’s 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, North Macedonia, where I joining dialogues o how too translate such initiatives from ambition to implementation - scaled through digital, financial, and human capital:
 
1️⃣ Digital Transformation
AI forecasting, smart grids, and digital twins are redefining how power systems are planned and operated. enabling predictive maintenance, dynamic balancing of renewables, and lower system costs.
 
2️⃣ Financial Reform
Redirecting fossil-fuel subsidies, still over USD 1.5 trillion globally, toward clean energy and social protection can unlock regional capital for distributed solar, e-mobility, and efficiency retrofits.
 
3️⃣ Youth Leadership
Young innovators are designing the next generation of clean-energy solutions. Their work shows that innovation ecosystems will drive the transition. #EnergyForDevelopment #UNDP #JustEnergyTransition #Digitalization #EnergyFinance

🎙️ Peter David Pedersen , Co-Founder and Executive Director, NELIS Global

	•	Youth empowerment and opportunity creation
	•	Equity, justice, and inclusion

*A Conservation Success Story: The Resilience of Sea Turtles*

Sea turtles have long fascinated humans with their ancient lineage and majestic presence in our oceans. However, their numbers have been declining due to various threats, including overconsumption, bycatches, pollution, and habitat destruction. Nevertheless, the story of sea turtles on Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles offers a beacon of hope, demonstrating that with protection and conservation efforts, it is possible to reverse declining trends and rebuild populations. Let's explore this remarkable conservation success and the lessons it holds for protecting our planet's precious wildlife.

*A Story of Resilience and Conservation*

On Aldabra Atoll, protective measures introduced in 1968 have yielded impressive results, with over 15,000 egg clutches recorded annually between 2014 and 2019. This represents a staggering 500% increase since the 1960s, with an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 green sea turtles visiting the beaches each year to lay eggs. 

The Aldabra experience showcases the effectiveness of local conservation efforts, which can make a real difference in protecting species, while also highlighting the need for national agreements and international regulations to address broader threats.

Our Global #MultidimensionalPoverty Index 2025 with the Oxford Poverty & Human Development Initiative (OPHI), University of Oxford is out NOW. 

This new research finds that of 6.3 billion people in 109 countries, 1.1 billion are multidimensionally poor.

Poverty is still our greatest global challenge, which is also a challenge compounded by the climate crisis.

Of the 1.1 billion multidimensionally poor people, 887 million live in regions which are exposed to at least one of four climate hazards: high heat, drought, floods, and air pollution. 

Many poor people face overlapping climate hazards. 651 million live in regions exposed to two or more of these climate hazards, and 309 million in regions exposed to three or four climate hazards.

As climate hazards continue to grow in frequency and intensity, countries which currently have higher multidimensional poverty levels will likely experience greater average temperature increases. It is vital to align poverty reduction efforts with climate action. In the face of the climate crisis, our commitment is clear: no one must be left behind.

Read the full report below and learn more via our Human Development Report Office - United Nations Development Programme: https://go.undp.org/ioE

From New York Climate Week to Building Bridges, Geneva — and onwards to COP30, Belém

At the 2025 #UNGA and #ClimateWeek in New York, I was struck by the growing momentum around real solutions—those that can transform lives and protect our planet.
Among the most overdue breakthroughs: clean cooking is finally on the global agenda.

At the #SDG7ActionForum, Sheila Oparaocha of #Energia and Heather Adair-Rohani from #WHO reminded us that “clean cooking” barely captures the grim reality of dirty cooking:
- 3.2 million premature deaths every year, mostly women, more than malaria, TB, and HIV combined.
- Girls and women are risking violence while spending hours collecting firewood.
- Families trapped by the cost of charcoal, LPG, or kerosene.
- Devastating health impacts, deforestation, and biodiversity loss.

As Riad Meddeb of #UNDP noted, the case for clean cooking is undeniable:
- Dirty cooking drains US$1.4 trillion annually in health and productivity losses.
- Only 1% of clean-energy investment targets clean cooking.
- 2.5% of global greenhouse emissions come from dirty cooking, the same as the aviation sector.

There’s no reason for this to continue. The technology exists—the missing ingredients are political will and financing at scale.

At #bloomberg hosted event Mary Schapiro, Catherine McKenna, María Mendiluce reminded us of the power of women in leading for climate change. Women-led innovation should answer the call of 400 million women to access clean cooking solutions. 

As Åsa Skogström Feldt of IKEA and Yasmina Zaidman of Acumen said at #ActionSpeaks, community engagement and trust are the catalysts that make social change unstoppable, but it takes time.

Enter CleanStove.org. We are proving that the future of clean cooking is community-led, off-grid, solar-powered, and battery-driven induction: ruggedized, reliable, smoke-free, and sustainable.

Each CleanStove® enables unlimited cooking in daylight, plus up to four hours after dark, with built-in LED lighting, USB charging, and eSIM-enabled smart monitoring. The feedback from women using pilot stoves in India, Senegal and Tanzania says it all: “It's a miracle”. 

At #BuildingBridges in #Geneva, another critical link emerged: clean cooking and high-integrity carbon credits. Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Artificial intelligence is advancing at an extraordinary pace — opening a frontier that demands both imagination and responsibility. On one hand, AI holds immense potential to reshape our world. On the other, Earth’s life-support systems — climate, biodiversity, and water — are under unprecedented strain, and meeting these challenges will require ever more energy.

Global energy demand grew by 2.2% in 2024 — nearly double the recent decade’s average — with electricity consumption jumping by 4.3% as electrification, heat waves, data centers, and digitalization surged. Over the 2025–2027 period, electricity demand is expected to keep rising at around 3.9% annually.

In 2024, AI consumed 415 TWh of electricity — more than 150 individual countries. By 2030, global data center demand could reach 945 TWh, exceeding Japan’s total electricity use. Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live without reliable access to energy.

This poses an important question: what kind of intelligence are we building? Can AI learn from nature to design future energy systems that deliver a just transition?

In a reflection co-authored with Riad Meddeb , we explore the idea of Planetary Intelligence — the integration of human, technological, and natural systems to sustain habitable conditions.

Synchronize energy with the planet’s balance - AI can move beyond optimizing data centers to orchestrate energy flows as nature does — cutting grid losses, balancing renewables in real time, reducing emissions by up to 10% by 2030, and unlocking 175 GW of additional transmission capacity.

Integrating planetary health into our energy systems for smarter societies - When designed to mirror natural systems, AI can help manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity — generating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while preserving the ecosystems that sustain life.

Advancing an inclusive and equitable energy future -  From tracking bird migrations around wind farms to developing over 40 African language models, AI can amplify diverse voices and ensure that the energy transition becomes not only smarter — but also fairer and more resilient.

If AI is trained on the principles that govern life on Earth, it can help us see both the forest and the trees — guiding us toward an energy future that is more intelligent, more just, and more human.

Read more about planetary intelligence in our recent publication on Illuminem: https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

If you want to really understand both the synergies and tensions between #GreenHydrogen and #Development, there are 3 outputs you MUST read. 

1. 'Development strategies for the green hydrogen economy in emerging economies' by Fabianna Bacil, Anthony Black, Marina Domingues, Jun Jin, Rasmus Lema, Glen Robbins, Sören Scholvin. Available here: https://lnkd.in/ezcHwRpS

2. The United Nations report 'Navigating currents of Green Hydrogen Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework', by UNDP & TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, authored by Riad Meddeb, Pavel Bilek and I.
https://lnkd.in/e63jWxgb

3. 'Dismantling green colonialism: energy and climate justice in the Arab region', a book edited by hamza hamouchene and Katie Sandwell, which focuses on the politics of green extractivism with detailed cases across the Arab world. https://lnkd.in/eJK3cC2U

All three pieces are quite complementary. The first focuses on the sectoral choices and strategies pursued by different countries (Brazil, Chile, China, and South Africa) and explains differences in policies and outcomes. The second one links green hydrogen with human development needs, across energy access, environmental degradation and industrialisation, highlighting how developing nations can avoid the first mover disadvantage at the height the learning curve for H2.  The third one bring the political economy angle, the unevenness and dependencies that can created under current conditions and behaviours in green energy sectors, and provides cases that require careful examination with global relevance.

Green hydrogen can be a force for good or a terrible thing for humanity, developing nations and the planet. Whether it is one or the other will depend on how we collectively shape this agenda over the next decade.

It's been a couple of months of sabbatical so far. While I'm still doing a couple of things for Alameda Institute as needed, this time on official leave is allowing me to catch up on a lot of things and finalise some strategic aspects of my current research projects.

I'm working on three book manuscripts. Now that the edited collection on land connections and struggles in Palestine is almost done, I get to focus again on my original manuscript on ecological transitions from a Global South perspective (which is long overdue to my publisher at Grupo Planeta , but I promise will be worth the wait). In the meantime, I'm also revising the topic of my first book from 2019 for Grupo Editorial Record to provide an update on the status of political fragmentation in Brazil, something very necessary given the still constant threat to our democracy.

But I'd like to share some other things that are already out.

1. The special issue of NACLA report, which I co-edited with my friend and dear colleague Breno Bringel . Titled "Green Capitalism in the Americas", it presents excellent pieces of research on the threats of false solutions and the opportunities for just alternatives when it comes to climate change. Our introduction is available here: https://lnkd.in/dwGjwQ_d (A few articles are open access, but as a member of the NACLA editorial board, I also encourage people to subscribe, since we do put out great issues every year!)

2. I was invited to write this piece for The Break Down on the dilemmas faced by Brazil to really advance its climate leadership. Considering that, historically, our emissions come mostly from land use change and deforestation, caused by dispossession and aggressive monoculture practices by agribusiness, it is impossible to take our NDCs and pledges seriously while landowning class continues to wreak havoc, including by controlling our Congress. https://lnkd.in/eHw6mzFq (it's a beautiful issue too, I highly recommend it)

Green hydrogen has been hailed as the “fuel of the future” and now 58 countries & regional blocs have already adopted hydrogen strategies - half of them in developing economies. The market, now valued at nearly USD $8 billion in 2024, could grow eightfold by 2030.

But major challenges persist. Land and water demands are steep; costs remain high; and dependence on critical minerals adds new risks. Without careful governance, the green hydrogen economy could risk reproducing extractive models and leaving developing countries exposed to technological disruptions.

That’s why Riad Meddeb , together with Amir Lebdioui and Pavel Bilek of the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford , co-authored this latest policy-brief: “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework” to address these challenges.  The brief introduces the ‘3P Framework’ to guide countries in shaping hydrogen pathways that deliver inclusive development:

🙏 People: Expand energy access, build resilient systems & support a just transition.

🌍Planet: Safeguard land, water, biodiversity & critical minerals through strong governance.

📈Prosperity: Phase investments, strengthen industrial policy & foster local value chains.

Unlocking the potential of green hydrogen is becoming one of the defining opportunities in the global shift toward sustainable energy systems. With the the right policies, safeguards and context-specific strategies in place, it can become a real driver of just transitions and shared prosperity.

It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sustainable energy can be a true lever for human development.
 
At a time when cooperation is under strain, sustainable energy remains one of the most powerful levers for progress - creating jobs, powering schools and clinics, advancing gender equality, and building resilience. Because in the end, the energy transition is never only about megawatts; it is about people and communities. Yet with 666 million people still without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking, we must rethink where and how we act. That is why three priorities stand out:
 
⚡️ Clean cooking at scale - 2.1 billion people still cook with polluting fuels. Scaling clean cooking is not just about energy access, it is about saving lives, empowering women, and protecting the planet.
 
⚡️ Development assessment for a just transition - A just transition means linking energy to jobs, health, education, and resilience, so every investment delivers tangible benefits for people and communities.
 
⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableEnergy #CleanCooking #AIforDevelopment

Years of accelerating investments in renewables energy systems are paying off. Solar is now 41% cheaper than fossil fuels, and nearly 100 new climate commitments were announced last week at #UNGA80 . Yet as geopolitical tensions and intensifying climate shocks threaten energy security, we must move beyond targets to build systems that are resilient by design.
 
🔗 Read more in the new Sustainable Energy Bulletin: The Era of Energy Security 👉 https://lnkd.in/exUQY3mf This priority of energy security was highlighted during a high-level dialogue during UNGA80 on Ukraine’s energy recovery which underlined that solidifying a green and decentralized energy system is an imperative for national security. Similarly, public and private actors reaffirmed their commitment to Mission 300 for accelerating energy access that is not only accessible but also affordable and reliable.
 
But the finance bottleneck for resilience persists: countries and companies have pledged $1.6 trillion by 2030 under Energy Compacts, yet less than 0.1% of global climate finance goes to adaptation in energy systems. We must make resilience bankable - turning protection of people and infrastructure into an investment case at scale. The future of energy security will also hinge on innovation and optimization - exactly where the triptych of digital, data, and AI is central. AI-driven risk modeling, paired with robust analytics and digital platforms, can help investors and policymakers optimize targeted financing where it is most effective.
 
As we head toward #COP30 in Brazil, progress will be measured not only by how quickly we transition to renewables but by how resilient and inclusive those systems are.

Crises from wars to climate were a key energy theme at the 80th General Assembly and New York Climate Week. In this bulletin, the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub discusses how to build resilient energy systems to achieve energy security. Innovation abounds in the Global South; from China's vehicle-to-grid pilots to the Caribbean's regional parametric insurance facility. 

It has never been more clear the role energy plays in both stabilizing crises situations and longer-term development. Extreme heat drives demand for cooling systems that prevent illness; shifting rainfall patterns make powered solutions like precision irrigation and desalination important for stable food and water systems. With sustainable energy, countries can protect and advance development gains across health, food and water systems, education, and jobs, particularly for those most vulnerable to climate impacts. 

From this year's flash floods in South Asia that destroyed energy infrastructure, to last year's droughts in Latin America and southern Africa that reduced hydropower capacity - the time to build resilience into energy systems is now.

New Multilateralism: A Global South Perspective
In my latest article on Medium, I argue that the system created in 1945 is running out of road—paralyzed by veto politics, skewed finance, climate injustice, and digital monopolies. The Global South is charting a path toward a New Multilateralism that is more inclusive, just, and peaceful.

For the South, this crisis is not abstract—it is lived reality:
⚠️ Debt distress
🌱 Climate vulnerability
💻 Digital exclusion

Financing the Blue Economy involves a combination of private and public capital, often channeled through specialized financial instruments like blue bonds and blended finance mechanisms. This includes integrating blue economy criteria into existing financial systems, supporting blue economy activities through targeted investments in sectors like sustainable fisheries and renewable energy, and using ocean-focused financial products such as blue bonds, debt-for-nature swaps, and impact investing. Achieving this, requires collaboration between governments, financial institutions, and corporations to establish clear standards, transparent governance, and a strategic shift in capital allocation towards ocean health and economic growth. 

In a recent article, Belinda Bramley points to the critical role of banks in encouraging and then enabling investors to finance Blue Economy initiatives. As an example, she points to Asian Development Banks new incubator, which supports sovereign and corporate borrowers who have plans to offer blue bonds. In a keynote address at an event in 2021, organised by the same bank, I was able to add insights based on my own experience.
Another example - still at a formative stage - is the World Bank's Blue Economy toolkit to establish a development framework that is clear and can be universally applied. Although the Blue Economy is still a relatively new concept, and potential investors remain wary of committing the very large sums that are called for, there are different ways in which banks can help to build confidence. At different levels - international, regional, national and local - and from different sources of capital.
Bramley believes that banks can help to release much-needed investment. If the Blue Economy is to achieve its undoubted promise, much will depend on the ability of banks to achieve this.

Over and above the actions of different financial agencies, there is the underlying issue of a disparity between rich and poor nations. This is a theme which recurs throughout this book, reflecting the fact that the fulfilment of Blue Economy aspirations will fall well short if there is not a correcting mechanism to enable all parts of the world to invest.
Different nations have fallen behind in economic development, often through no fault of their own, and it is in the interests of all to
provide a more level playing field. The Blue Economy will not be achieved without this kind of recognition .

Green hydrogen has been hailed as the “fuel of the future” and now 58 countries & regional blocs have already adopted hydrogen strategies - half of them in developing economies. The market, now valued at nearly USD $8 billion in 2024, could grow eightfold by 2030.

Without careful governance, the green hydrogen economy could risk reproducing extractive models and leaving developing countries exposed to technological disruptions.

That’s why Riad Meddeb , together with Amir Lebdioui and Pavel Bilek of the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford , co-authored this latest policy-brief: “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework” to address these challenges.  The brief introduces the ‘3P Framework’ to guide countries in shaping hydrogen pathways that deliver inclusive development:

🙏 People: Expand energy access, build resilient systems & support a just transition.

🌍Planet: Safeguard land, water, biodiversity & critical minerals through strong governance.

📈Prosperity: Phase investments, strengthen industrial policy & foster local value chains.

Unlocking the potential of green hydrogen is becoming one of the defining opportunities in the global shift toward sustainable energy systems. With the the right policies, safeguards and context-specific strategies in place, it can become a real driver of just transitions and shared prosperity.

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.

public_card_text:
What is “planetary intelligence”?

In this new thought piece, Riad Meddeb and Stefano Pistolese define it as “the planet’s capacity to sustain habitable conditions through the integration of life, technology, and natural systems.”

It’s a powerful idea, with potential to catalyze a new paradigm in development - an ontological shift which sees our systems as interlinked and adaptive, with AI as a mirror to how nature processes complexity.

The AI future we are working to - optimizing energy systems in alignment with natural resource management - involves a global and distributed system of interconnected digital models, each based on a system of sensors and satellites, working to maximize human development potential while limiting climate impact. This sounds familiar, though, right? This is the same underlying logic of how our natural world functions. 

So, if “planetary intelligence” is to guide practice, let’s make sure we define it right. There are multiple lenses that can we use:

🔹 Planetary Intelligence as Distributed Cognition
Planetary intelligence isn’t a single brain, but millions of actors - from local communities to AI to forests and rivers - each contributing to resilience. Here, AI’s role is to amplify local decisions as part of a global network of feedback.

🔸 Planetary Intelligence as Optimizing within Boundaries
Intelligence as the ability to detect and respect limits - carbon budgets, water tables, biodiversity thresholds.

♦️ Planetary Intelligence as Temporal Feedback
Intelligence as the ability to link present actions with long-term planetary consequences. AI must embed ecological memory, ensuring decisions today safeguard generations to come.

How we define planetary intelligence will shape whether it remains a metaphor - or becomes a practical guide for the AI era.

Yesterday at a #UNGA80 side event on Data, Digital Transformation and the Resilience in the Energy Transition, I discussed a defining question for the AI era:
 
AI is already reshaping the #energy transition - but does it build resilience, or deepen fragility?
 
Last year, in Mexico’s drought-stricken Querétaro region, farmers rationed water and lost crops. Just a few kilometers away, billions were invested in new AI data centers requiring extensive water cooling systems. The paradox is striking.
 
By 2027, data centers are projected to consume nearly 900 TWh of electricity and 6.6 billion cubic meters of water annually, largely driven by AI. But at the same time, AI also holds promise: it can optimize renewable grids, enable faster climate forecasting, and unlock billions in private finance for clean energy in the Global South.
 
During the discussion, youth delegates asked powerful questions:
👉 Are we using #AI in a way that advances sustainable energy for all?
👉 How can we prevent AI from becoming another burden on already stressed systems, and instead ensure it can create real opportunities for development?
👉 Will we step up to govern our energy transitions, so they are not only resilient, but also just?
 
The answers will define whether AI accelerates the clean energy future - or becomes another burden on already fragile systems. #UNGA #AI #EnergyTransition #Resilience #Sustainability

public_card_text:
Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.

“Powering Inclusive Growth from Potential to Prosperity: Opportunities and Trade-offs in Green Hydrogen” 

Grateful to @Yu Zhuoping, Amir Lebdioui , @Zhu Yongsheng, @Wang Ju, and @Zhang Jinxuan, who joined me at our UNDP and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) high-level dialogue to explore how Asia-Pacific can ensure hydrogen drives inclusive growth, not just exports. 

But will incurred green hydrogen truly deliver for development? By 2050, green hydrogen could supply 12–22% of global energy demand, with Asia-Pacific at the center. The market, worth USD 8 billion today, could grow nearly eightfold by 2030. To get there, challenges around water (9 liters per kg), land (30,000 hectares of solar per million tonnes), and costs ($4.5–12/kg) must be managed, while scaling low-carbon hydrogen beyond today’s 1% share. And here, three priorities emerged from our discussion.

1️⃣ Align with development priorities: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, cut costs, and create jobs. If treated only as an export, communities risk being left behind. 

2️⃣ Embed safeguards: Large-scale hydrogen needs land, water, and minerals. Strong governance is vital to prevent water stress, land conflict, and inequality. 

3️⃣ Lead through cooperation: Regional partnerships on standards, infrastructure, and finance can amplify Asia-Pacific’s voice and build local value chains and skills. 

We explore these opportunities and trade-offs in more depth in our latest policy paper - Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: 🔗 https://lnkd.in/e7f_tvA9 At @UNDP, we believe the real promise of green hydrogen lies not in the technology alone, but in the choices we make today to ensure it drives inclusive, sustainable development for all. #EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #InclusiveGrowth

Grateful for the opportunity to join colleagues at @UNDPChina country office to to discuss how our new UNDP Strategic Plan 2026–2029 puts sustainable energy at the center of development; not just as an enabler, but as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve itself. 

China’s experience shows why this matters. With 47% of global wind & solar; 20M EVs (half the global fleet); and having already achieved its 2030 renewables target six years early, China is proving that transitions can be nationally transformative and globally catalytic. But ultimately, this is not only about megawatts; it is about people, communities and systems for shared prosperity. 

In our dialogue, I shared three priorities for deepening China’s leadership and expanding shared progress: 

🔹 South–South and triangular cooperation
With 25 regional projects totaling 12 GW of new capacity worth $5B under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and partnerships across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, China is extending its leadership. The next step is moving from projects to scalable solutions grounded in governance, safeguards and inclusion. 

🔹 Digital, data & AI for energy systems
With grid investment projected at $100B annually and data center demand set to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030, China is pioneering AI forecasting, digital twins and open data. Embedding these innovations into just transition frameworks is essential to ensure they deliver inclusive benefits 

🔹 Energy as a lever for human development 
As set out in the new Strategic Plan, success will not be measured only in megawatts, but in human outcomes: schools and clinics with reliable power; farmers with modern tools; households with clean cooking; and communities with greater resilience to crisis. 

At UNDP we are proud to work alongside China and global partners to connect innovation with governance, finance, and inclusion. A just energy transition is not only a national achievement – it's a shared global responsibility. The real challenge is not how fast we expand renewables, but how effectively we connect them to the people who need them most. #EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #China

"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." 

This was at the heart of the dialogue that I co-convened with GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) on “Bridging the Gap  Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.” 

We meet at a moment of paradox. Global clean energy investment will reach $2.2 trillion this year, yet less than 15% flows to developing economies outside China, and Africa, with its vast renewable potential, receives only 2% of that total. The challenge is not if the transition will be financed, but how - and whether it will be just, inclusive, and development-maximizing. From our panel session, three priorities came through strongly: 

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership
From Africa’s green industrialization agenda to Asia-Pacific’s blended finance models, countries are already pioneering ambitious national strategies. The task now is to scale and aggregate pipelines to attract capital at the level required. 

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale  
Sovereign green bonds in Indonesia, sukuk in the Middle East, and guarantee facilities in Africa show how innovative instruments can unlock billions. The next step is replication and mainstreaming. 

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success. 

Grateful to Khaled Sharbatly , @Wang Yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin for their insights, and to @Beate Trankmann for reminding us that speed without fairness risks leaving people behind. 

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it delivers for people first: lighting homes, powering schools and opening opportunities across the Global South. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

It was a real pleasure to meet with my friend Dr. Gloria Magombo, Permanent Secretary for Energy and Power Development in Zimbabwe, to reflect on how Zimbabwe can accelerate its energy transition in ways that put people, resilience, and prosperity at the center.
 
Our discussion touched on three priorities that are vital to unlocking this transformation:
 
🇿🇼 Supporting Zimbabwe’s National Clean Cooking Strategy With nearly 62% of the population still without access to clean cooking, and rural access below 10%, the new National Clean Cooking Strategy is more than an energy plan. It is a health plan, a gender equality plan, and an environmental plan. UNDP stands ready to support its implementation with policy expertise, innovative finance and local delivery models.
 
🇿🇼 Mission 300 Zimbabwe’s ambitious compact under Mission 300, targeting 100% electricity access by 2030 and raising clean cooking access to 70%, is a milestone moment. Building on our Solar for Health and mini-grid initiatives, UNDP is committed to helping ensure these targets translate into real, reliable services for households, clinics, schools and enterprises.
 
🇿🇼 South–South cooperation and financial instruments Closing Zimbabwe’s annual energy gap - which currently costs the country 6.1% of GDP - requires innovative finance and regional collaboration. Instruments like the Renewable Energy Fund show how blended finance and South–South learning can unlock scale and inclusion.
 
Zimbabwe’s journey shows that energy is not only a national priority, it is a shared responsibility. By linking ambition with action, and innovation with inclusion, we can ensure the transition delivers for those who need it most. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #CleanCooking #Mission300 #SouthSouthCooperation #Zimbabwe

It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sustainable energy can be a true lever for human development.
 
At a time when cooperation is under strain, sustainable energy remains one of the most powerful levers for progress - creating jobs, powering schools and clinics, advancing gender equality, and building resilience. Because in the end, the energy transition is never only about megawatts; it is about people and communities. Yet with 666 million people still without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking, we must rethink where and how we act. That is why three priorities stand out:
 
⚡️ Clean cooking at scale - 2.1 billion people still cook with polluting fuels. Scaling clean cooking is not just about energy access, it is about saving lives, empowering women, and protecting the planet.
 
⚡️ Development assessment for a just transition - A just transition means linking energy to jobs, health, education, and resilience, so every investment delivers tangible benefits for people and communities.
 
⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableEnergy #CleanCooking #AIforDevelopment

Delighted and an honor to deliver the keynote at the Opening Ceremony at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing on behalf of UNDP - a gathering that comes at a pivotal moment for the global energy transition.

One message stood out clearly: clean energy is no longer tomorrow’s promise. It is today’s most powerful tool for jobs, growth and true energy security. In 2023, the sector employed 16 million people worldwide, with China alone accounting for 7.4 million - nearly half the global total. By 2030, clean energy and efficiency could generate 70 million new jobs, with each $1 million invested in renewables creating nearly three times more jobs than fossil fuels

The shift is already reshaping economies. In 2023, clean energy accounted for 10% of global GDP growth - rising to 20% in China and nearly one-third in the EU. The question now is not whether the transition is happening, but how fast we can scale it and how effectively we can ensure its benefits reach the people who need them most.

It was in this context that @UNDP and @GEIDCO announced a new MoU: a commitment to deepen collaboration on innovative finance, South–South cooperation and digital solutions that can accelerate a just and inclusive energy transition.

We stand at a moment of great possibility. Clean energy is not only about megawatts—it is about unlocking opportunities to create millions of new jobs and livelihoods. It is a driver of transformative change across our societies, reshaping how we live, produce, and connect. And with the power of digital tools, data, and AI, we can ensure energy security that is smarter, more resilient, and inclusive. Together, we can build an energy future that truly leaves no one behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SouthSouthCooperation #GEI2025

The much-awaited UNDP report mapping the extractivist traps, technological risks and developmental opportunities from #GreenHydrogen is finally out. 

As things stand, the green hydrogen economy risks reinforcing historical extractive patterns and heightened exposure of developing nations to tech disruptions, while failing to deliver broad-based development benefits. 

This report 'NAVIGATING THE CURRENTS OF GREEN HYDROGEN', published in collaboration with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, and which I had the chance to co-write with Riad Meddeb and Pavel Bilek, proposes a “3P” framework - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to ensure that hydrogen strategies align with human development goals. 

For People: Projects must not consume renewable-based electricity for H2 exports that would otherwise be destined for local populations and instead bring energy additionality to expand energy access, build resilient electricity systems, and support labor upskilling to enable a just transition. 

For the Planet, we must avoid a decarbonization that leads to other types environmental degradation. Governments need strong internal environmental appraisal and regulations to address GH2 risks around land, water, biodiversity, and intense critical minerals use. Such regulations help avoid adverse environmental impacts and social injustices in the communities and ecosystems where GH2 is produced.

For Prosperity, though many countries seek to position themselves as first movers in the green hydrogen sector (Chile, Namibia, etc.), given the uncertainty surrounding future market demand and the rapid pace of technological disruptions, a cautious experimental approach may be more appropriate for many fiscally-constrained developing nations, where lessons from early entrants can inform more cost-effective and scalable hydrogen development strategies at more mature stages of the hydrogen learning curve. Governments must integrate hydrogen into strong technology foresight assessments and a coherent industrial policy to promote local value addition while guarding against technological obsolescence.  

Ultimately, green hydrogen is not a development guarantee but a policy choice.

"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." 

This was at the heart of the dialogue that I co-convened with GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) on “Bridging the Gap  Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.” 

We meet at a moment of paradox. Global clean energy investment will reach $2.2 trillion this year, yet less than 15% flows to developing economies outside China, and Africa, with its vast renewable potential, receives only 2% of that total. The challenge is not if the transition will be financed, but how - and whether it will be just, inclusive, and development-maximizing. From our panel session, three priorities came through strongly: 

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership
From Africa’s green industrialization agenda to Asia-Pacific’s blended finance models, countries are already pioneering ambitious national strategies. The task now is to scale and aggregate pipelines to attract capital at the level required. 

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale  
Sovereign green bonds in Indonesia, sukuk in the Middle East, and guarantee facilities in Africa show how innovative instruments can unlock billions. The next step is replication and mainstreaming. 

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success. 

Grateful to Khaled Sharbatly , @Wang Yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin for their insights, and to @Beate Trankmann for reminding us that speed without fairness risks leaving people behind. 

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it delivers for people first: lighting homes, powering schools and opening opportunities across the Global South. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

Financing the Blue Economy involves a combination of private and public capital, often channeled through specialized financial instruments like blue bonds and blended finance mechanisms. This includes integrating blue economy criteria into existing financial systems, supporting blue economy activities through targeted investments in sectors like sustainable fisheries and renewable energy, and using ocean-focused financial products such as blue bonds, debt-for-nature swaps, and impact investing. Achieving this, requires collaboration between governments, financial institutions, and corporations to establish clear standards, transparent governance, and a strategic shift in capital allocation towards ocean health and economic growth. 

In a recent article, Belinda Bramley points to the critical role of banks in encouraging and then enabling investors to finance Blue Economy initiatives. As an example, she points to Asian Development Banks new incubator, which supports sovereign and corporate borrowers who have plans to offer blue bonds. In a keynote address at an event in 2021, organised by the same bank, I was able to add insights based on my own experience.
Another example - still at a formative stage - is the World Bank's Blue Economy toolkit to establish a development framework that is clear and can be universally applied. Although the Blue Economy is still a relatively new concept, and potential investors remain wary of committing the very large sums that are called for, there are different ways in which banks can help to build confidence. At different levels - international, regional, national and local - and from different sources of capital.
Bramley believes that banks can help to release much-needed investment. If the Blue Economy is to achieve its undoubted promise, much will depend on the ability of banks to achieve this.

Over and above the actions of different financial agencies, there is the underlying issue of a disparity between rich and poor nations. This is a theme which recurs throughout this book, reflecting the fact that the fulfilment of Blue Economy aspirations will fall well short if there is not a correcting mechanism to enable all parts of the world to invest.
Different nations have fallen behind in economic development, often through no fault of their own, and it is in the interests of all to
provide a more level playing field. The Blue Economy will not be achieved without this kind of recognition .

⚡️Renewables are out-investing fossil fuels—cheaper than ever!
Such an honour to serve my third year on the UN Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition (#CEET) and to attend the Annual Forum, hosted by the GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) alongside the #GlobalInterconnectedConference 2025 (#CNCC, Beijing). 🙏 Heartfelt thanks to our Chinese colleagues at #CEET and #GEIDCO for the warm hospitality and remarkable experiences.
The forum opened with a welcome from Isaac Elizondo Garcia, remarks by Mr Ciyong ZOU (UNIDO) and Mr Cheng Zhiqiang (#GEIDCO), followed by reflections from Semida Silveira and ULF Larsson (CEET new co-chair). The tone echoed the UN Secretary-General’s call for a “supercharged surge” in renewables: investment now exceeds fossil fuels, and costs are lower—e.g., recent figures show solar PV ~41% cheaper and offshore wind ~53% cheaper than fossil fuel generation.
A highly experienced and motivating panel followed with Mr Riad Meddeb (UNDP), Mr James Wahogo (Eastern African Power Pool), Mr Hongpeng Liu (#UNESCAP), Ms Divya Kottadiel (Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL)), Mr Pedro Jatobá (GEIDCO, Brazil), and Professor Dr. Phoebe Koundouri (#SDSN).
Key takeaways
- Put people first: energy access, jobs, health, gender equity, and resilience must anchor every decision.
- Close the finance gap: de-risking, Energy Transition & Investment Plans, and performance-based models can unlock scale.
- Think regional: interconnected grids, shared planning, and standards cut costs and boost resilience.
- Don’t overlook clean cooking & distributed solutions: huge health and development gains.
- Universities & networks (e.g., SDSN): force multipliers for skills, data, and visibility.
I was glad to contribute to two high-impact levers:
- Energy conservation & efficiency—the fastest, cheapest first fuel.
- Circular economy—direct and indirect GHG cuts across value chains. As Circular Economy Engagement Coordinator with The SMEP Programme at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), I shared our Bangladesh textiles case on circular wastewater reuse, which drew strong interest. Full report: https://lnkd.in/gYie9HRW 
We also caught a glimpse of China’s rapid robotics advances—from agile “robot dogs” to boxing-capable humanoids—signalling a new era that can support (and challenge) how we work.
Now, time to recharge for tomorrow’s Global Interconnected Conference 2025. Special thanks to Frank, Shuguang Qi, and all local colleagues for making the event so special—and a big shout-out to our CEET online participants whose late-night dedication was truly inspiring.

This is our moment of opportunity.” - António Guterres  
 
The clean energy future is no longer a promise, it’s a fact. The latest Unitednations secretarygeneral  synthesis report, Supercharging the New Energy Era - with contributions from UNDP  and partners - captures this global momentum and sets out what’s needed to turn it into lasting, inclusive progress. The full report is available here: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e_HHrGzg 
 
In 2024, renewables accounted for over 90% of new power capacity. Solar and wind are now the most affordable options in many markets. Battery storage has increased more than 40 times since 2015. Clean energy jobs now outnumber those in fossil fuels. These are not isolated achievements; they’re signs of growing global readiness to scale sustainable energy solutions that support the SDGs. 
 
Yet we face a dual challenge: “The energy transition is unstoppable. But the transition is not yet fast enough or fair enough.” Fossil fuels still dominate supply. Less than 20% of clean energy investment reaches the Global South - where it’s needed most. To turn momentum into inclusive, sustained progress, the report outlines six priority actions to keep the 1.5°C target within reach and ensure no one is left behind. 
 
1️⃣ Align policies: Ensure coherence, clarity, and certainty by integrating energy, climate, and economic policies to accelerate a just transition. 
  
2️⃣ Build infrastructure: Modernize grids, expand storage, and develop digital and physical systems to support a 21st century clean energy economy. 
  
3️⃣ Power growth with renewables: Meet rising electricity demand - especially from AI and data centers - with clean, affordable renewable energy. 
  
4️⃣ Center people and equity for a just transition: Put communities first by ensuring fair access, job creation and inclusive development in all transition efforts. 
  
5️⃣ Expand global cooperation: Strengthen trade, investment and innovation partnerships to supercharge deployment and reduce costs worldwide. 
  
6️⃣ Unlock finance for the Global South: Dismantle barriers to affordable capital and scale energy-transition investments to $1.4–1.9 trillion annually in EMDEs.

Investments and exports are soaring in clean-energy tech such as #solar and #EVs. That’s not just good for the planet - it’s powering over 16 million green #jobs and reshaping the global #economy. 

Here’s what to know: 
 - Clean energy investment topped $2 trillion in 2024
 - Low-carbon exports hit $1.1 trillion
 - Millions of new jobs created - and growing
 - US, EU and China are leading the charge.

The World Economic Forum’s latest Energy Transition Index ranks the efforts of 118 nations on clean #energy progress. Overall the data points to a greener future, showing the most collective progress since 2021. But trade disputes and global tensions could easily stall momentum, and a gap remains to the $5.6 trillion needed for net zero.

💥 Debt-for-climate and debt-for-nature swaps are often hailed as “innovative” ways to address both debt distress and development finance. In practice, they systematically underperform on both fronts. Udaibir Saran Das makes this point clearly with excellent examples in his new piece, "Do debt swaps deliver on development finance?" https://lnkd.in/e3SmeC56 His analysis highlights exactly why these debt swaps fall short and why the underlying diagnosis matters.

The underlying problem is misdiagnosed. Most developing countries are not insolvent—they are illiquid. (This is one area where I slightly diverge from Mr. Das’s analysis, which frames many countries as insolvent. But in many cases, the issue is not an inability to repay over time, but rather the mismatch between short-term debt obligations and long-term development returns.) They face debt distress not because of reckless borrowing or weak fundamentals, but because they can only access capital on terrible terms: short maturities and high interest rates. Why? Because of structurally biased credit rating methodologies that penalize countries for being poor, even when they are high-growth, creditworthy markets.

We explain these structural factors in our Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment paper on Lowering the Cost of Capital in EMDEs https://lnkd.in/eJYAh6WN (co-authored with Jeffrey Sachs Ana Maria Camelo Vega and Bradford M. Willis )

These swaps purport to unlock capital, but they don't in any way unlock the structural barriers to affordable capital. Instead, they:
• Mobilize a tiny fraction of the finance actually needed for climate or nature, let alone the Sustainable Development Goals
 • Deliver negligible debt relief 
 • Impose significant transaction costs—up to 25% of the total—largely enriching intermediaries
 • Often require offshore control structures that constrain national sovereignty
 • And, perversely, may even trigger credit downgrades or negative outlooks by rating agencies for looking too much like a default.

Debt swaps are not a credible or effective tool to address the debt crisis or to mobilize critical finance. If we are serious about solving either of those challenges, we should start by understanding the (interrelated) root causes and then focus on ensuring EMDEs have access to long-term, affordable finance, including from global capital markets.  And for existing debt, accumulated over decades under these discriminatory systems, we should at the very least restructure it to align with the long-term growth trajectories of rapidly growing EMDEs.

(Thanks to Paul DeNoon for sharing the article!).

public_card_text:
We face an unprecedented moment, in a time of geopolitical challenges, but also one of unprecedented momentum in the global energy transition. The transition is no longer a question of ‘if’ - but of how fast, how fairly, and how securely we can collectively achieve it. Cost-competitive renewables are a reality.
 
Great honour to launch IRENA’s "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024" report side by side with the United Nations in support of United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres's "Moment of Opportunity" speech today. During #HLPF, I informed Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed of the continued cost leadership of renewables in global power markets.
 
The addition of 582 gigawatts of renewable capacity in 2024 led to significant cost savings, avoiding fossil fuel use valued at about USD 57 billion. 91% of new renewable power projects commissioned last year were more cost effective than any new fossil fuel alternatives. 
 
In total, in 2024, renewables helped avoid USD 467 billion in fossil fuel costs, reinforcing their role not only as the lowest-cost source of new power but also as a key driver of energy security, economic stability, and resilience in a volatile global energy landscape. This achievement is the result of years of innovation, policy direction, and growing markets. 
 
However, this progress is not guaranteed. Rising geopolitical tensions, trade tariffs, and material supply constraints threaten to slow the momentum and drive-up costs. To safeguard the gains of the energy transition, we must reinforce international cooperation, secure open and resilient supply chains, and create stable policy and investment frameworks. 
 
The transition to renewables is irreversible, but its pace and fairness depend on the choices we make today.

Read the full report 👉 http://bit.ly/4506Eg6
Watch the UN SG’s “Moment of Opportunity” speech 👉 http://bit.ly/4kOC2Eg

public_card_text:
While 92% of the world now has electricity, over 666 million people—mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa—still live without it. More than 2.1 billion continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels.

Meanwhile, clean energy investment surpassed $2.2 trillion in 2024, overtaking fossil fuels for the first time. Yet, only 15%—excluding China—reached the Global South. The moment is now to redirect capital where it’s needed most.

Energy is a powerful enabler of transformative change—for people, planet, and prosperity—and the Global South is increasingly at the forefront of this energy revolution.

At the HLPF, it was an honor to represent the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub at The Future of Energy – Comprehensive Sustainable Energy Solutions for the Global South, organized by Sustainable Development Solutions Network in collaboration with the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) . I had the pleasure of discussing how we can accelerate a just energy transition with Prof. Vijay Modi , Elizabeth Nelson , Mr. MEI Feng, Prof. Peter Oviroh , and Mr. Eric F. In 2024, global energy demand grew by 2.2%, exceeding the average growth rate of the past decade—with over 80% of that growth driven by emerging and developing economies.

Progress is accelerating across three key areas:
1️⃣ Integrated energy planning – Kenya’s digital mapping helped expand electricity access from 20% to 75% in just eight years.
2️⃣ Innovative finance and policy de-risking – Mechanisms like feed-in tariffs and concessional capital are cutting financing costs by 25–30%.
3️⃣ South–South cooperation – Now representing over 28% of global trade, it is unlocking faster, more inclusive energy access and investment.

UNDP is proud to work with partners—like Mission 300—to close the energy access gap and accelerate a just, inclusive transition.

These solutions are already transforming lives. The question is no longer if they work, but how fast and how far we can go.

Together, we can turn ambition into fair, equitable, and lasting impact.

With the potential to reduce 5.4 GtCO₂e annually by 2035, AI can become central in low-carbon transitions, if deployed equitably.
 
By aligning national energy master plans, digital transformation strategies and investment frameworks, these solutions can become powerful drivers of systemic change to shape a more just and sustainable future.

Rethinking Fossil Fuel Subsidies: A Lever for Transformative Change in Transport and Society

In Latin America and the Caribbean, fossil fuel subsidies consumed 0.6% - 1.3% of GDP between 2015 and 2021. While traditionally aimed to reduce energy costs for the population, they often fail to reach the most vulnerable and entrench high-emission transport systems.

It’s time to shift the narrative: Fossil fuel subsidy reform is not just a matter of fiscal discipline; it is a strategic development opportunity.

New analysis from UNDP LAC Latin America and Caribbean  and UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub outlines a three-step roadmap for governments to redirect subsidies toward low-emission public transport systems that are cleaner, more inclusive, and economically sustainable:

1️⃣ Build strong policy frameworks: Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Ecuador are embedding clean transport into national strategies through transparent fuel pricing and targeted reforms.

2️⃣ Invest in clean mobility: Uruguay’s MOVÉS initiative subsidizes electric buses up to $55K/year. Colombia provides tax incentives for low-emission vehicles. Paraguay links public subsidies to service quality standards.

3️⃣ Mobilize institutions and people: Cross-sector coordination and public engagement are making reforms more equitable, resilient and politically feasible.

Redirecting fossil fuel subsidies is about more than budget reform; it’s a catalyst for long-term social transformation. Sustainable transport systems can improve air quality, reduce inequality and create green jobs across the region.

Find out how @UNDP is supporting countries in delivering this transition: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBRWe5Rm #EnergyForDevelopment #FossilFuelReform #SustainableTransport #LatinAmerica #DevelopmentFinance

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth. #EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

Solid-state batteries offer significant advantages that align with global sustainable development priorities:
 
1️⃣Enhanced Performance and Safety:
SSBs provide higher energy density; faster charging times; and improved thermal stability, reducing risks associated with lithium-ion batteries. Their robustness across temperature ranges and extended lifespans also make them ideal for grid-scale energy storage, facilitating greater integration of renewable energy sources and enhancing grid resilience.
 
2️⃣Cross-sectoral Innovation:
The compact size and enhanced performance of SSBs present opportunities beyond EV applications including: electric aviation, shipping and even consumer electronics, enabling longer operational life and increased safety.
 
3️⃣Environmental Sustainability:
By minimizing reliance on flammable liquid electrolytes and reducing the demand for scarce minerals, SSBs contribute to lowering the environmental footprint of battery production and disposal, supporting circular economy principles.
 
The global push for solid-state battery innovation reflects a broader truth: clean energy transitions are no longer national ambitions, they are shared imperatives. Strategic investments from India, research partnerships between Brazil & Singapore, and cross-sector collaboration signal a growing recognition that technology must serve inclusive, sustainable development.
 
Solid-state batteries hold the promise not just of better performance, but of decarbonizing mobility, strengthening energy resilience, and accelerating progress toward SDG7. Energy access is not just a technology challenge; it’s a matter of equity, regional cooperation, and economic opportunity.

Globally, 685 million people still lack access to electricity—80% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the current pace, 660 million people could remain unelectrified by 2030, the vast majority in Africa. This is not merely a technical gap; it’s a development crisis that impacts health, education, livelihoods, and resilience.

But this is also a moment of unprecedented opportunity.

Africa holds extraordinary clean energy potential. Countries like Ethiopia and the DRC possess over 80 GW of hydropower potential, while the Sahel region enjoys some of the highest solar irradiance on Earth. Yet, between 2002 and 2020, Africa received less than 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewable energy. Cross-border electricity trade remains limited, with just 10 GW of transmission capacity—compared to 127 GW in Europe.

This raises a critical question: how can we close the energy access gap without reinforcing inequality and fragmentation?
The answer lies in a just, integrated energy transition—where regional power trade becomes a catalyst for shared prosperity. And the solutions are within reach:

1️⃣ Invest in Cross-Border Infrastructure:
Regional power trading can reduce electricity supply costs by up to 30%, accelerating access in underserved areas. In the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), countries like Namibia and Botswana are already importing affordable hydropower from Zambia and Mozambique, enhancing both affordability and reliability.

2️⃣ Mobilize Inclusive Finance & Guarantees:
Bridging Africa’s $25 billion annual clean energy investment gap requires more than capital. Concessional finance, de-risking mechanisms, and technical assistance are critical to enabling LDCs to participate in regional markets and scale up electrification.

3️⃣ Leverage Regional Comparative Advantage:
Countries such as Ethiopia and the DRC generate more clean power than they consume, and the Sahel’s solar potential exceeds 2,200 kWh/m²/year. Regional trade allows these countries to monetize surplus energy, promote industrialization, and generate revenues that can support local development.

This is a defining moment. The energy access challenge is no longer just about generation—it’s about connection, cooperation, and coordination. With the right policies and targeted investments, Africa can shift from energy poverty to regional power prosperity, while advancing climate action and inclusive growth.

 ✅ How to overcome high capital costs for solar in small island markets

➡️ In Indonesia, the Youth Co:Lab initiative supports youth-led enterprises delivering solar cold storage and clean cooking to last-mile communities. 

➡️In Uruguay, a public-private AI training program is scaling in public schools - preparing students for careers in energy, agriculture and logistics. 

➡️In the Dominican Republic, a national AI strategy is helping youth gain digital skills and launch small enterprises. 

Local innovation ecosystems must bridge the gap between energy, data, and jobs. Countries that invest in distributed renewable energy, open-source data platforms and localized AI training programs are better positioned to build domestic markets for AI-enabled services. 

This is not just a development challenge; it’s a strategic opportunity. With the right investment in energy, skills, and ecosystems, we can drive the AI and clean energy transitions from the ground up. 🌊 As we mark #WorldOceansDay and the launch of the 2025 UN Ocean Conference in Nice, we have a pivotal opportunity: to align ocean health with the global energy transition.

The ocean is a foundation of life on Earth. It covers 75% of the planet; generates 50% of our oxygen; absorbs 30% of CO2 emissions; and supports +150 million jobs worldwide. It provides food, energy and critical resources to billions - yet remains under threat from rising temperatures, acidification, pollution, overexploitation and biodiversity loss.

If the ocean economy were a country, it would be the fifth largest economy in the world. That level of economic and environmental significance calls for bold, integrated responses. Here’s where development action can accelerate meaningful impact:

1️⃣ Decarbonize Maritime Transport as a Catalyst for Clean Energy Systems:
Maritime transport emits over 1GtCO2 annually (around 2.9% of global emissions) and is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize due to fossil fuel reliance and long asset lifecycles. To align with the Paris Agreement, zero-emission fuels need to make up 5% of international and 15% of domestic shipping by 2030. Transitioning to clean fuels can transform shipping from a major emitter into a catalyst for clean energy investment, innovation, and industrial demand, contributing directly to system-wide decarbonization and reducing global GHG emissions by 3-5% by 2030. 

2️⃣ Transform Ports into Clean Energy Hubs for a Just Transition:
Strategic clean fuel corridors can anchor renewable deployment, storage and grid upgrades at ports - especially in Small Island Developing States, where ocean-based exports account for 16% of GDP. Port electrification enhances climate resilience, connects maritime and energy planning, and ensures vulnerable economies benefit from the energy transition.

3️⃣ Integrate Maritime Decarbonization into Global Energy Finance:
Despite their potential, maritime and ocean-based clean energy solutions remain underfunded. In 2022, global clean energy investments reached  $2.1 trillion; yet < 1% was directed towards maritime energy developments. Offshore wind alone could grow from $39.6B in 2024 to $146B by 2031, powering up to 1.5B homes annually by 2050 and driving inclusive growth across coastal regions - especially in the Global South. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can unlock scalable pathways for maritime decarbonization and clean energy innovation at sea.

Decarbonization is critical, not only for SDG 13  and SDG 14, but for resilient, inclusive development. 

As we look toward this 2025 UN Ocean Conference, we must raise ambition; align public and private finance; and unlock innovation across the blue economy. A healthy ocean is not only vital for biodiversity. It is fundamental to a just energy transition

The ocean cannot wait - and neither can we. #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #MaritimeDecarbonization #SDG14

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth. #EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

🌊⚡️What if the world’s smallest nations could lead the next big energy revolution?
 
At a marine testing site in Scotland, 20 Oyster wave energy converters have the potential to power 12,000 homes. Now imagine the transformative potential if Small Island Developing States (SIDS) - surrounded by ocean, rich in wave and tidal resources - could harness these innovations at scale?
 
Ocean-based energy technologies are fast becoming a practical solution to some of the world’s most pressing challenges: energy security, climate resilience and economic development. For SIDS, which face some of the highest energy costs globally, and are among the most vulnerable to climate change, these technologies offer a triple win; sustainable power, economic opportunity, and strengthened resilience.

With a combined global wave and tidal energy potential of over 55,000TWh/year, here’s how SIDS are already driving system-wide changes with how they manage & benefit from their blue economies:
 
🔹 Tonga is developing a 10-MW wave power park in Tongatapu - set to meet 50% of its energy needs and cut emissions by 20%.

In 2024, the world added over 585 GW of renewables, and clean energy jobs surpassed 16 million. Solar is now the least expensive electricity source in history and global energy investments are expected to reach $3.3 trillion by 2025. This is more than a technology shift; it's a global economic transformation.
 
But one critical question remains: Are we making the energy transition work for everyone, everywhere?
 
In Mongolia, coal still dominates the energy system. In Ulaanbaatar, 1.6M people rely on raw coal for heat - driving pollution 27x over WHO limits, causing 7,000+ premature deaths and costing 10% of GDP.  Despite these challenges, Mongolia has committed to change - targeting 30% renewable energy by 2030.
 
That’s why, at the recent Multistakeholder Workshop on Advancing a Just Energy Transition in Mongolia - co-hosted by Mongolia’s Ministry of Energy and UNDP - I shared four ways on how to reposition these challenges as opportunities for a just and inclusive transition:
 
1️⃣ Finance That Unlocks Scale:
By 2023, Mongolia attracted $533M across 12 utility-scale renewables. However renewables in Mongolia face high capital costs and limited de-risking. Green bonds, sovereign guarantees, and blended finance (like Paraguay’s $150M e-bus model from $20M in seed funding) can mobilize clean energy investment at scale.
 
2️⃣ Urban Energy That Protects Lives:
Coal-based systems drive both pollution and inequality. Ulaanbaatar’s air crisis is a public health emergency. A just transition must deliver clean heating, efficient housing, and e-mobility. UNDP pilots show solar + battery + insulation can cut emissions and protect over half the country’s population.
 
3️⃣ Digital Tools for Smart Equity:
Energy demand grew 4.7% per capita in one year. Mongolia’s vast geography needs digital planning. AI and geospatial tools - like smart meters in Chingeltei that track carbon savings -can guide clean energy to off-grid and low-income areas, just as UNDP is doing in Moldova.
 
4️⃣ Fossil Fuel Subsidy Reforms:
In Mongolia, fossil fuel subsidies reached $9B in 2023; a 120% increase since 2018. Yet by fully phasing them out, we could free up 3.6% of global GDP for reinvestment. With UNDP’s support, countries like Mongolia are designing reforms that reinvest from e-mobility to human capital and health systems.  
 
A just transition is about people, not just power. It’s about shaping a future where energy delivers jobs, health, resilience and dignity. Across Mongolia and Asia-Pacific, @UNDP is helping make that future a reality, ensuring no one is left behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #Mongolia #GreenFinance #DigitalForDevelopment
