Today, I am raising the alarm.
 
Together with the Troika of COP28 UAE, COP29 Azerbaijan, COP30 Brazil Presidencies and the Global Renewables Alliance (GRA), IRENA published a report that tracks progress towards tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.

And as the custodian agency tasked with tracking and reporting on progress towards 2030, IRENA concludes that progress falls short. 

The landmark #UAEConsensus agreed at COP28 is critical for our global efforts to keep 1.5°C within reach but we are at risk of missing our collective goal.

Some key facts:

1- Despite an unprecedented growth in renewable power additions of 473 GW in 2023, it is far from enough. The world must add on average 1044 GW every year. 

2- Current Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) will only add 1.5 TW of renewable power capacity by 2030, but we need more than 7 TW.
 
3- Global investments in renewables reached a record of USD 570 billion in 2023 but it must triple to USD 1.5 trillion annually. 

Furthermore, current investment patterns are disproportionately concentrated in advanced economies and a few large emerging markets like China, India, and Brazil. The rest of the developing world remains underserved, receiving just 10% of global energy investments. This imbalance threatens not only the pace of energy transition but also the equitable distribution of its benefits.
 
It is still possible to achieve our goals, but it requires immediate global action to overcome the structural and systemic barriers that impede progress. Significant progress is needed across key enablers of the energy transition, namely: infrastructure and system operation, policy, supply chains and skills, finance and international collaboration. 

The next round of NDCs in 2025 must close the gaps. And an agreement on a robust New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) of climate finance at COP29 will be vital for enhancing financial support for climate action in the Global South.

Read ‘Delivering on the UAE Consensus: Tracking progress toward tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030’ that was released today at the PreCOP to inform national delegations and negotiators in the run up to COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. 👇

The Many Facets of Energy Transition: From India to the World

While the world has made progress in renewable energy deployment, with over 40 per cent of the world's electricity generated from zero-carbon sources (Source: BloombergNEF), taking clean energy to the last mile remains a problem. 

However, India, which ranks fourth globally in renewable energy installed capacity, stands out as a pioneer in the Global South with its energy transition story.  It has facilitated access to clean cooking fuels for over 96 million women in merely three years; the rural electrification programme has brought electricity to over 28 million households in a span of two years. The rooftop solar programme launched this year, ‘PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana’, aims to bring the benefits of solar energy to 10 million households across rural and urban areas. 

What lessons can the world take from India’s citizen-centric, sustainable, clean energy transition? How does access to clean energy intersect with other factors such as health, gender, and economic progress?

Our session with @SEforALL at UNEnergy’s #SDG7 Action Forum delved into these questions. Swipe to see what our speakers said!

public_card_text:
Today, 600 million people in Africa still live without electricity. 

Studies have shown it is the best predictor of whether someone can escape poverty. The Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative has highlighted the correlation between lack of electricity access and poor health, unemployment, malnourishment, and more. 

To address this, I am honored to announce that The Rockefeller Foundation is supporting Mission 300 (M300), an initiative of the World Bank Group and African Development Bank (AfDB) to provide electricity access to 300 million Africans by 2030. 

Alongside the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet (GEAPP), the @Rockefeller Foundation is committing an initial $10 million for the Mission 300 TA Accelerator, which will boost the projects needed to double the current pace of electrification on the continent.

Former U.S. Government Head of the Power Africa initiative, @Andrew Herscowitz, is also on board to help steer the M300 effort. 

We believe that by identifying innovative solutions, working with additional partners, and measuring our progress in initiatives such as M300, we can help African leaders usher in a period of green, inclusive growth. #PoweringAfrica

In recent years, amid alarming geopolitical turmoil and a global pandemic, the inherent vulnerabilities of traditional energy sources have been starkly exposed to the developed world. 

For many developing nations, however, price volatility, supply shortages, and geopolitical dependencies are not temporary disruptions but enduring realities. 

The transition to a renewables-based energy system addresses many of those issues, moving energy dependencies from the global to the regional level and making most countries less susceptible to geopolitical disruptions. 

However, while energy security options will become more diverse, the energy system will also grow more complex, given the wide range of technologies and participants involved. 

As governments make substantial investments in infrastructure that is increasingly electrified, digitalised, and decentralised, it is essential that decision makers do not simply transpose outdated paradigms from the fossil fuel era onto these emerging systems.

IRENA's report, "Geopolitics of the Energy Transition: Energy Security", explores specific issues that should be systematically considered to guide national decision-making in navigating the existing and emergent challenges of a highly complex and integrated new energy system. 👇

Over the past year, our group of experts - from the 'Digitalization in Energy' Task Force at United Nations Economic Commission for Europe | UNECE Sustainable Energy , which I co-chair together with Elizabeth Massey - has documented several case studies. 

These studies demonstrate that only through the practical application of previously researched theoretical concepts we can fully grasp both the benefits and limitations of digitalization in the energy sector.

The upcoming compendium presents five case studies from different geographies, each addressing unique challenges and opportunities within the digitalization of energy systems. By exploring these case studies, we aim to bridge the gap between theory and practice, showcasing both successful implementations and areas where improvements are needed.

🌟🛖 Yoboki village is approximately 50 km from the town of Dikhil, located in the southwestern part of Djibouti. This community of around 2,000 residents, spread across 400 households, is embarking on a transformative energy journey with the Africa Minigrids Program (AMP). The country's project coordinator highlighted this at the recent national dialogue hosted by UNDP, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, and the Ministry of Energy.

Currently, Yoboki relies on a diesel-powered generator with a capacity of 100 kVA to provide electricity. The distribution network serves about 250 households, offering intermittent power for only 6 hours daily. This setup supports essential needs such as lighting and ventilation, but the existing generator's capacity is insufficient, leading to frequent voltage drops and equipment failures.

Read on about the full assessment, which led to AMP engaging the community and selecting the location for minigrid development.

The severe floods in Pakistan in 2022 damaged 22 power plants and caused outages and load shedding of up to 16 hours. 

In the face of severe climate change, we must leverage the power of digital technologies and innovation to ensure energy resilience and security. Here is how:

* Smart grids and AI-driven storage enhance grid stability, reliability, and efficiency
* Advanced analytics and smart meters optimize energy use, empowering consumers with real-time data for more efficient consumption and cost savings
* IoT and Digital Twins (DT) provide real-time monitoring and proactive maintenance, ensuring infrastructure resilience and rapid response to extreme weather events

For the first time in over a decade, the number of people without electricity is rising, with Sub-Saharan Africa bearing 83% of this global deficit. Africa🌍 is engaging in an #EnergyRevolution to unlock its potential.

I am absolutely honored to be selected as an IRENA Youth Delegate for 2024. 
 
I am thrilled to be among the 100 IRENA Youth Delegates from 60 different countries, The New Generation of Decision Makers at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Youth Forum at the 14th IRENA Assembly in Abu Dhabi, UAE. 
The program kicked off with a welcoming session led by the Director-General of IRENA and esteemed guests, followed by panel discussions covering various topics focused on fostering engagement in key technological advancements, building capacity for #youth at the core of the energy transition, providing #opportunities for youth to play a key role in #IRENA's mission of accelerating #renewableenergy deployment, achieving climate objectives, and advancing the #sustainable development agenda.

Over the first days of the forum, we had an enlightening introduction on topics in #finance, #science, #social, and #policy aspects in renewable energy. We had presentation about introduction to renewable energy by Cesar Barraza-Botet, PhD  covering renewable energy sources from solar to wind, hydrogen, and new innovations in the sector. Other sessions included skills development for the energy transition by Samah Elsayed, discussions on ESGs and Social Corporate Responsibility for a just energy transition by AbdelRahman Fahmy  and Asma Rouabhia, and skills youth need in developing renewable energy projects and proposals by AbdelRahman Fahmy and David Arinze 

On the second day of the forum, I attended the session with IEEE , Advancing Technology for Humanity works on #AI for #DigitalInnovations in Energy transitions with speakers Sajith Wijesuriya, Krishna Ajith  and  Cybele Ghanem.    

The Forum continued with a panel discussion including #AcceleratingYouthLedInnovationandEntrepreneurshipinCleanTechPanel, with panelists, Grace Nanteza, Asma Rouabhia, Nourhan Algharabli, Benjamin Keller  and Shreshth Mishra, who shared the challenges and barriers faced by youth-led innovations. 

There inspiring thoughts, experiences, and advice addressed the true skills that all young changemakers  need to have, emphasizing the importance of being ready to #failfast, Having the #courage to continue until we achieve success as well as creating as many #connections as possible. 
I had the opportunity to share about renewable energy projects to  powering agriculture and the potential of #Agrivoltaics,  integrating the  #food production and #energy generation, the Food-Energy-Water nexus.  

The IRENA Youth Forum were filled with #encouragement with inspirational closing by from Riccardo Toxiri and Riad Meddeb.  I look forward to the #IRENAAssembly and the #FutureEnergyForum in the coming days which IRENA Youth delegates have the opportunity to meet with global leaders, government representatives, and IRENA experts.

#AI for #ClimateAction- A balancing act between opportunities & perils of artificial intelligence in #climatechange. 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn
 
I am excited to share my new podcast on “AI solutions for Cimate Actions & Insights from #COP28 with @Carina Schuster 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn  
@Sci-Tech Suisse Podcast
 
AI can do great things to fight climate change:
 
✅ The use of data-driven AI solutions can produce starting results in the fight against climate change
 
✅ Data and AI platforms can be powerful instruments to predict weather, track #GHG emission or develop targeted strategies against #airpollution or support the protection of #biodiversity and endangered #species

✅ AI tolls can accurately predict the #deforestation of #rainforest and loss of biodiversity though the analysis of aerial photographs and #satellite data

✅ AI can be used to enhance the #sustainability of #agriculture, lower #airpollution or reduce negative environmental impact of infrastructure projects
  
AI can become a huge problem for climate change:
 
✅The use of AI technologies is expected to grow exponentially with the expected growth of the current global AI #market size of around $200 billion U.S. dollars to reach over 1.8 trillion U.S. dollars by 2030.

✅ #Machinelearning and the training of AI #algorithms require huge amount of computing power and #electricity

✅ The #computing #power required for AI applications, such as recognizing & processing images and vast among of data increased 300,000-fold from 2012 to 2018.

✅AI and #Deeplearning require huge amount of high-quality data and increasingly huge computing power and data #infrastructure

✅The training one AI model using a single high-end graphics card (#gpu ) generates the carbon equivalent of a flight across the United States or 626,000 pounds of carbon dioxide (MIT Technology Review

Huge Public Investments in AI for Good is needed to leverage the power of AI for climate action

✅ Increasingly AI models require and deep learning require huge computing power driven by specialized computer chips- called GPUs

✅ The costs of the needed AI infrastructure in the form of hyperscale #datacenters and data infrastructure are becoming huge

✅ Whereby #bigtech companies, such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft are investing billions into AI the public sector, research institutions and universities don’t have the necessary resources to make the necessary huge investments

✅ AI can only be unleased for climate action through public sector investments, since the big tech companies are purely focused on commercial applications of AI

✅ A large boost in public concessional #climatefinance is needed since only a very small part of private sector investments go into the development of AI models for the public good & AI to for climate action.

#tech #tech4good #deeptech @Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH @Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)

As the year comes to a close, I would love to reflect on a period marked by remarkable achievements and meaningful progress with the Arab Youth For COP . This year has been a testament to the dedication, resilience, and impact of our initiative as we achieved a significant milestone. Our delegation, comprising ten fellows from various Arab countries, effectively implemented our programs, a testament to our commitment to climate action and sustainable development. The journey to COP28 UAE  was enriched by our pre-conference efforts, notably our participation in the #menaclimateweek held in Riyadh. The successful implementation of our programs and the meaningful engagement of our 10 fellows at COP28 underscore our commitment to representing diverse voices, especially those from regions facing conflict, occupation, or marginalization.

Central to our preparatory phase were comprehensive capacity-building sessions. These sessions, led by experts like Mr. Kamal Djemouai  on negotiation principles and Riad Meddeb  alongside his team at the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub, focused on just transitions and green jobs. But also some sessions on leadership skills sessions by other partners. This groundwork was crucial in equipping our fellows with the necessary skills and knowledge to navigate the complexities of climate negotiations and advocacy.

At COP28, our primary focus was on fostering meaningful engagement for our current fellows as well as alumnus. We created platforms enabling them to voice the concerns and aspirations of their communities.This approach ensured that diverse perspectives were represented and heard, an essential aspect of inclusive and effective climate action.

As we conclude this year’s mission, our eyes are set on the future. We are already laying the groundwork for next year’s initiatives. We are deeply committed to sustaining and expanding our programs, and in this spirit, we are open to exploring partnerships and collaborations. 

We believe that through collective effort and shared knowledge, we can create a more sustainable and equitable future. Therefore, we warmly invite you to join us in this endeavor. Your support, be it through expertise, resources, fund, capacity building, or advocacy, would be invaluable in our journey towards a just greener, more resilient world. 

Absolutely, a heartfelt thank you is due to everyone who played a part in this year’s success. Our partners’ invaluable contributions and our fellows who deserve immense appreciation for their dedication and enthusiasm. And of course, a special acknowledgment to our own team Neeshad Shafi  Amal Ridene  and Omnia El Omrani, MD  Small in size but monumental in impact, each member’s dedication, creativity, and perseverance have been the cornerstone of our achievements.

This year of success is not just an end but a beacon for future endeavors, inspiring us to continue our journey with more vigor and determination.

Reflecting on #COP28 in Dubai, it's evident that the conference signifies a crucial starting point, but substantial efforts are still imperative to avert a 1.5°C temperature rise. The urgency transcends mere negotiations; it underscores the need to secure financing promptly for a swift transition to a decarbonized world.

At the core of achieving decarbonization objectives lies the imperative to minimize risks and their associated costs, emphasizing the pressing nature of the situation. The clarion call is unequivocal—intensify endeavors in renewables, triple efficiency, and substantially augment climate finance.

Acknowledging the magnitude of the challenge, reliance on public finance alone proves inadequate. This is an all-encompassing moment that requires collaboration with both multilateral and national development banks to strengthen their role in channeling and delivering climate finance along with domestic and international public and private finance. Equally pivotal is the active engagement of the private sector in steering this transformative journey. 

On the COP sidelines, discussions with officials from Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Maldives, Nepal, Ethiopia, Vietnam, Zimbabwe, Senegal, Azerbaijan and Togo, along with UNDP representation at key events, underscored a shared vision for change. From elevating ambitions in NBSAPs to championing nature-based solutions and just energy transformation, the common thread is clear—change is possible and already underway.

In essence, post-COP28, we stand at the threshold of transformative action, and the next steps demand collective commitment and collaborative action from all stakeholders to turn the tide towards a sustainable and decarbonized future.

With a robust $5 billion portfolio, UNDP actively collaborates with 140 countries on nature, climate, and energy initiatives. Our work with civil society organizations and Indigenous Peoples will be crucial for these efforts. 

Let’s work together to expedite progress, success hinges on the urgency of our responses.

📢 Our new Deloitte Thought Leadership paper on financing the energy transition is now available online. In this paper, we study the reason why the investments in the green technologies are below what is needed to stay in line with climate goals and we identify the key policy and financial tools to boost these investments, especially in developing economies. 

💡 The analysis in this paper goes beyond finance to help provide a holistic overview, employing quantitative modelling and qualitative assessment of the technology landscape, policy environment, and financing challenges, without missing the geographical dimension.

📰 My key takeaways:
▶Governments, investors, and financial institutions must work together to  reduce risks and unlock private capital at attractive costs, especially in developing economies, where about 75% of the investments should take place.
▶While significant upfront investments are needed (4.3% to 5.7% of global GDP in the short run), the cost of inaction is even higher (8% of global GDP).
▶Improved financing structures could reduce the cost of the transition by 25% (US$50 trillion) over the period to 2050. 

🔗 Click on the following link to find out more about the study: https://lnkd.in/gtqkud_A 🤘 Bravi to my co-authors: Bernhard Lorentz Johannes Trüby Pradeep Philip Clément Cartry Clémence Lévêque Vincent Jacamon Will Symons Brice Chasles Dr. Gildas de Muizon Freedom-Kai Phillips

History was made on the first day of the UN Climate Conference, #COP28 . UNDP Maldives welcomes the historic agreement to operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund and funding arrangements and acknowledges the unwavering efforts made by Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) and the Maldivian Government with its members of the transitional committee who worked tirelessly to get us to this point.

In conjunction with this momentous development, we are delighted to present a new paper titled 'Loss and Damage and Climate Litigation: How Can the Maldives and other Small Island Developing States (SIDS) Position Itself for Greater Climate Action.' Authored by UNDP Maldives in collaboration with Frankfurt School of Finance & Management , the paper advocates for a unified climate governance strategy, empowering vulnerable SIDS like the Maldives with reforms and strategic options to embrace this innovative instrument of climate justice now in action.

The paper explores the critical nexus between climate-related loss and damage and the recent surge in climate litigation. It argues that SIDS should lead robust and equitable climate action, navigating the complex relationship between climate change, human rights, and legal responsibilities. The paper advocates for enhanced funding for SIDS, rooted in the principles of loss and damage, utilizing both traditional and novel financing mechanisms.

The recommendations within the paper urge #SIDS to spearhead climate resilience initiatives, employing innovative financial and insurance strategies. It underscores the need for exhaustive data collection and risk assessments to strengthen early warning systems and devise disaster risk strategies. To effectively manage and foresee climate litigation risks, it calls for educational initiatives on climate liability, incentivization of private sector adaptation, and harmonization of national legal frameworks with environmental pledges.

The overarching aim is to develop a cohesive approach that integrates financial risk management, climate adaptation, and active engagement in the development of international climate finance mechanisms. While primarily intended for the Maldives, the insights also hold relevance for other nations.

Last month, a BIG news came out of the palm oil industry, with significant (positive) implications for the wider agri-commodities sector!

The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) announced the appointment of a tripartite consortium comprising of leading agritech firms Agridence , CIED , and NGIS “to develop a unified, bespoke Certification, Trade, and Traceability System (CTTS)”.

The keyword here – at least for me – is ‘traceability’, which has been a longstanding challenge for the industry. This is because of complex supply chains and difficulties in tracking palm oil from small-scale producers, who make up a large part of the commodity production.

RSPO’s revamped digital system would essentially aim to streamline and integrate RSPO’s sustainable palm oil certification, audit, and risk assessment processes into a secure trading platform, enabling end-to-end traceability of palm oil.

This comes as a major relief to palm oil corporates, who are under pressure from the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), which will come into effect from December 2024. EUDR mandates that importers of deforestation-risk commodities (e.g., palm oil, cocoa, timber, natural rubber) and their derived products into the EU market must be able to prove that the products do not originate from recently deforested or degraded land.

The new system to be developed by the consortium, led by Singapore-based Agridence, could be instrumental for demonstrating the sustainable origin of RSPO-certified palm oil, especially from major producers Indonesia and Malaysia. The system will leverage Agridence’s experience and expertise from building a similar platform for the natural rubber industry.

At Singapore Agri-Food Innovation Lab (SAIL) , we are engaged in exploring innovations, learnings, and best practices from different industries and supporting their adaptation and adoption by our Corporate Partners and stakeholders to drive sustainability in the wider agri-food sector.

Last week, in collaboration with AUDA NEPAD, we hosted a working session in Stellenbosch for our project launched earlier this year titled “Africa’s Development Agenda for its Green Minerals”.

This project has brought together scholars to craft policy papers and briefs to analyze African governments' plans for mineral-driven industrialization and manufacturing. This included in-depth country case studies, exploring ambitious mineral strategies and their essential requirements, such as the DRC-Zambia battery industry MoU, South Africa's PGM endeavors, and Zimbabwe's lithium-powered ambitions.

The working session was a platform to discuss the findings and progress of the papers and chart the course for the next phase of the project.
A special acknowledgment to Mkhululi N Ncube from African Minerals Development  Centre  (AMDC) and Melaku Desta of Africa Trade Policy Centre at UNECA for their invaluable contributions as discussion facilitators.

Our gratitude goes out to Pamla Gopaul, Axel Rusenga, and Dr. Mustafa Sakr of AUDA NEPAD for pleasantly hosting us. We especially thank Saliem Fakir of The African Climate Foundation and Fred Kabanda of African Development Bank Group for their valuable presence.

A big thank you to our project leads, Dr. Olumide Abimbola, Patience, Amir Lebdioui, and all the contributors who have dedicated their expertise to this project.

We will continue to use this space to share project updates in due course!
